answer.evidence_in_the_data: The two labeled transfers are T1422 (80AD40250 -> 808C30740, 12,228.11 UK Pound, ACH, 2022-09-05 12:33) and T1870 (808C30740 -> 8100920E0, 50,878.02 Shekel, ACH, 2022-09-07 06:13). They form a two-hop chain through 808C30740, 41 hours apart. Two weak tells separate them from the surrounding traffic. First, they are the only ACH transfers that are both one-off and large. The other ACH rows are small recurring UK Pound payments (T1063, T1359, T1725, T2198, T2328 at 80.5 and T0721 at 79.46) or the 162,403.25 and 90,765.33 Shekel payments T0028 and T0340, which are not part of the labeled ring. Second, T1422 is the only transfer from 80AD40250 that is not the repeated 41,915.85 cheque to 80B2988C0, and it has a different recipient, currency and amount. T1870 is the only outflow of 808C30740 (1 sent versus 17 received). The amounts do not conserve across the hops, and the currency changes from UK Pound to Shekel, so nothing proves the same funds moved on. The identity of the ring cannot be confirmed from amounts, but the odd-one-out edges through the 808C30740 hub are visible. The loud candidates, 80FF95550 -> 8100920E0 at 32.9M cash and the 8100920E0 fan-out, are decoys. They are repeated and not labeled.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models anchored on the loudest structure, the repeated 32.9M cash hub 8100920E0 and its fan-out, and flagged those unlabeled rows. Others fell back to ordinary because the pass-through pairs do not conserve amounts and there is no loop. The two labeled transfers are a low-volume, cross-currency, non-conserving two-hop chain that looks like one more recurring edge. Only gpt-6-sol v1 found the exact pair, and it lost the finding once the code facts and the stricter amount-matching rules were added in v2 and later.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A chain can be only two transfers. Amounts need not match and the currency may change between hops. Look for a transfer into an account with very low out-degree (such as 808C30740, with one outgoing transfer) that is followed within 48 hours by that account's only outgoing transfer, especially if both are ACH and neither is a repeated identical payment. Do not require amount conservation for a two-hop chain.' Also remove the implied rule that pass-throughs must move nearly the whole amount.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact listing non-recurring edges, meaning transfers whose (from, to, amount) triple occurs exactly once, together with two-hop paths made only of such edges within 48 hours (here T1422 -> T1870). Rank these ahead of repeated-amount hubs. Optionally cap the flagged list to the one or two best candidates, to avoid flagging decoys like the 32.9M cash rows.
answer.risk_of_fix: Unique, non-recurring two-hop paths are common in ordinary traffic, so this will raise false alarms on neighborhoods where unrelated one-off transfers happen to meet at a low out-degree account. Dropping amount conservation also weakens the guard that stopped models from accusing busy hubs. Models may then flag both T1422 and T1870 in many ordinary neighborhoods.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1422 (80AD40250→808C30740) and T1870 (808C30740→8100920E0) form a time-ordered, two-transfer chain 41 hours 40 minutes apart. Both are ACH. T1422 is the only transfer on its account pair, and T1870 is 808C30740's only outbound transfer; together they bridge the otherwise largely separate Australian Dollar, UK Pound, and Shekel traffic. The rows do not show an exchange rate, balances, or proof that the funds received in T1422 funded T1870. The IBM labels themselves cannot be recovered from transaction attributes alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Many runs focused on the conspicuous 32.9 million Shekel cash deposits and 8100920E0's fan-out, flagging background transfers instead of the two labeled ones. Later runs noticed the T1422→T1870 path but treated mismatched currencies and amounts, or the absence of a loop, as grounds to reject a chain; the supplied pass-through examples also did not surface this 41-hour path. The v1 gpt-6-sol run identified both IDs, showing the path was visible without proving a fund-level link.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "For a chain, check time-ordered two-transfer paths within 48 hours; consider flagging both edges when they are nonrecurring ACH bridges and the intermediary's onward transfer is unique, even if amounts or currencies differ—describe this as a structural lead, not proof of fund continuity."
answer.system_fix: Add a second pass that enumerates all time-ordered two-hop paths within 48 hours, rather than displaying only a truncated pass-through list; rank paths by nonrecurring account pairs, a unique onward transfer, and whether both edges are ACH.
answer.risk_of_fix: A legitimate cross-currency payment through an account with one observed outbound transfer could meet the same test. ACH and bridge rarity should select paths for review, not establish laundering.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The three labeled transfers are T1909 (8018514B0 to 80AA72BA0, 4917.74 AUD ACH), T1230 (80AA72BA0 to 80AA72E10, 198.76 AUD ACH) and T2432 (80AA72BA0 to 8022AF930, 3593.22 USD ACH). They are the only transfers touching hub 80AA72BA0 that use ACH apart from the T0285 and T2300 neighbours, and they stand out from the rest of the rows. Every other transfer in the neighborhood is Cheque or Credit Card, and the 28 rows on the two repeating pairs are fixed-amount noise. T1909 comes in, then T1230 and T2432 go out to different counterparties in other amounts or currencies. T2432 goes on to 8022AF930, which sent T0285 (ACH, USD 4340.17) to 8022BACE0 earlier, so that fragment is also ACH and a currency switch. Amounts do not reconcile: 4917.74 in against 198.76 and 3593.22 out. So the shape is a small mixed fragment of IBM's longer stack, not a clean chain. Nothing in the amounts or graph alone marks it; only the ACH-versus-non-ACH split does, and that is a bench artifact rather than real behavior. The 80AA72BA0 to 80AD21FA0 stream (3569.09 and 12945.86) is recurring payments and not labeled.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Almost every model anchored on the two loud repeating pair streams, correctly read them as scheduled payments, and then dismissed the T1909 pass-through because amounts did not match, so they returned ordinary. The real ring is a few odd-format ACH transfers around the hub that are small and non-matching, and the code's pass-through pairs pointed almost entirely at the recurring 80AD21FA0 stream rather than at T1230 and T2432. The models that did say ring (mistral, kimi, glm) flagged the repeated streams as structuring, so they caught the labeled ids only by flagging 17 to 35 rows, which is wrong rows for the wrong reason.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'First set aside any sender-receiver pair that repeats the same amounts and formats on a schedule; judge the remaining one-off transfers on their own. A transfer that touches an account in the neighborhood but differs in format, currency or counterparty from that account's routine traffic, and sits in time-order with an inbound transfer to it (for example T1909 then T1230 and T2432), is worth flagging even when amounts do not match. List only those ids, not the recurring stream.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact that removes periodic fixed-amount pairs (same sender, receiver, amount, format repeated 3 or more times) and recomputes pass-through and chain facts on the residual transfers, listing the residual rows by id. Optionally add a fact marking transfers whose format or currency differs from the sender's modal format, since the ACH odd-ones-out are the signal here. Score on the residual graph as a second pass.
answer.risk_of_fix: Recurring-payment masking could hide a real scheme built on fixed amounts, and an odd-format flag will fire on any ordinary one-off ACH or foreign-currency payment from a business account, raising false alarms on ordinary neighborhoods. Because the ACH-only labeling is a bench artifact, a format rule would not transfer to real data.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: All three labeled transfers are ACH edges incident to 80AA72BA0: T1230 and T2432 leave it, and T1909 enters it. The only other ACH, T0285, does not touch that account. This isolates the labeled IDs as a candidate cluster, but does not prove laundering or trace funds: T1230 precedes T1909, and T2432 differs from T1909 in amount and currency.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models that missed the ring focused on the 28 recurring card and cheque payments and required a cycle or convincing amount-matched pass-through. They did not separately test the prompt's synthetic-data clue that every labeled transfer is ACH. Models that called a ring generally swept recurring payments into it; some also treated transfers in reverse time order as a chain.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'For this synthetic benchmark, inspect ACH transfers separately: if at least three ACH transfers share an account and include both incoming and outgoing edges, consider those ACH IDs as an other-pattern candidate; do not add non-ACH transfers or claim that an earlier outflow forwarded a later inflow.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed ACH-only incident-edge list by account. Here it would show 80AA72BA0 incident to T1230, T1909 and T2432, while T0285 is outside that cluster.
answer.risk_of_fix: An ordinary account with three mixed-direction ACH payments could be falsely flagged. The rule is a candidate-selection heuristic for this synthetic bench, not evidence that the same funds moved through the account.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair T1422 (80AD40250 -> 808C30740, 12,228.11 UK Pound, ACH, 2022/09/05 12:33) and T1870 (808C30740 -> 8100920E0, 50,878.02 Shekel, ACH, 2022/09/07 06:13) form a genuine two-hop chain: 808C30740 is the bridge account and T1870 is its only outbound transfer among 18 touches, ~41.7h after T1422. But nothing in the amounts or timing conserves value (12,228 GBP in, 50,878 ILS out, no stated FX link), the bridge also receives 17 other similar small inflows, and the chain is cut at both ends in this neighborhood. The only real tells are meta-hints from the bench: both labeled rows are ACH while the neighboring recurring traffic on the same corridors is Wire/Cheque/Credit Card/Cash, and both are one-off amounts on corridors otherwise dominated by exact-amount repeats (80.5, 103.85, 41,915.85). Absent the 'every labeled transfer is ACH' hint, the truth is not recoverable from rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models that flagged anything anchored on the visually loud structure (the three identical 32.9M Shekel cash deposits T0433/T2226/T2535 into hub 8100920E0 and the repeated 41,915.85 AUD cheques), which is exactly the recurring-payment background, so 24 of 26 runs flagged 0 of the 2 labeled ids. The models that looked for the chain (gpt-6-sol v2+, sonnet v3-v5, grok v2) rejected it because the computed pass-through facts highlight amount mismatch and zero loops, and the prompt's 'pass-through' framing taught them to demand amount conservation that a cross-currency, value-changing chain cannot show. Only gpt-6-sol v1 flagged exactly T1422+T1870, plausibly leaning on the ACH hint and the cross-cluster bridge, and the added code facts in v2 talked it out of that correct read.
answer.prompt_fix: Replace the pass-through criterion with: 'a chain is a path of two or more transfers through a bridge account; amounts and currencies need NOT match between hops (value may be converted, merged, or split) — weight instead (a) a bridge account whose outbound transfers are rare relative to its inflows, and (b) one-off amounts on corridors otherwise dominated by exact-amount repeats; treat identical repeated large transfers on one corridor as recurring traffic, not placement.'
answer.system_fix: Add two code facts per neighborhood: (1) for each account, out-degree rarity (e.g. '808C30740: 17 in, only 1 out: T1870'), which makes the bridge's single exit stand out; (2) an 'amount novelty' flag marking transfers whose exact amount appears only once on a corridor that otherwise repeats fixed amounts (would flag T1422 and T1870 and would NOT flag the 41,915.85 cheques or the 32.9M cash repeats). Optionally add a per-corridor format histogram so 'ACH on a Wire/Cheque corridor' is visible without the prompt leak.
answer.risk_of_fix: Relaxing amount-conservation will raise false positives on ordinary two-hop paths (this neighborhood alone has 20 pass-through pairs, e.g. 80A6EA1C0 -> 80AD40250 -> 80B2988C0), and the novelty flag would occasionally tag legitimate one-off payments like rent or invoices on otherwise repeating corridors; the 32.9M cash transfers would likely still attract attention as outliers even when labeled recurring.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair is a two-hop chain: T1422 is 80AD40250 -> 808C30740, 12,228.11 UK Pound by ACH, and T1870 is 808C30740 -> 8100920E0, 50,878.02 Shekel by ACH, 41.7 hours later. This is unusual in the neighborhood: 80AD40250 otherwise sends only AUD cheques to 80B2988C0 and receives small AUD amounts from 80A6EA1C0/80A190110, so T1422 is its only UKP ACH outbound; 808C30740's only outbound is T1870. The code-fact pass-through list includes the predecessor pair 80827DA70 -> 808C30740 -> 8100920E0, but the same logic should have surfaced T1422 -> T1870. It is only partly recoverable because amounts and currencies do not conserve and the neighborhood is dominated by noisy recurring clusters.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most v2+ models dismissed T1422/T1870 as ordinary because the two hops differ in amount and currency and there is no loop; many instead anchored on the huge 80FF95550 -> 8100920E0 cash fan-out (T0433, T2226, T2535) or the repeated AUD/GBP recurring payments, flagging rows that are not labeled. Models that used the computed pass-through facts still returned ordinary or hedged because the facts emphasize amount-conserving pass-throughs, and this chain is a short cross-currency fragment without amount conservation.
answer.prompt_fix: Add this rule: 'Do not require the same amount or currency for a chain. If account A makes a one-off ACH payment to B (not part of a repeated same-amount series) and B makes an ACH payment onward within 48 hours, list both transfers as a chain; in this data set the laundering rows are ACH.' This targets T1422/T1870 while excluding the repeated same-amount ACH series like 80827DA70 -> 808C30740.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact that computes two-hop ACH paths within 48 hours where the first hop is not part of a repeated same-amount series, and include those as 'cross-currency chain candidates' in the facts shown to the model (e.g., T1422 -> T1870).
answer.risk_of_fix: It will newly flag any one-off ACH followed by another ACH within 48 hours, such as legitimate supplier or payroll chains, and if the recurring-series exclusion is too weak it could still flag T1359/T1361 -> T1870.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The three labeled transfers T1230, T1909, T2432 share exactly two properties: they are the only three ACH transfers touching hub 80AA72BA0 (of 4 ACH in the whole neighborhood, the 4th being the isolated T0285), and they are the only transfers where 80AA72BA0 interacts with anyone other than its routine counterparty 80AD21FA0. T1909 brings in 4917.74 AUD from an outside account (8018514B0) that the hub never deals with again; T1230 (198.76) and T2432 (3593.22) push money out to two novel recipients (80AA72E10, 8022AF930). So the real signal is not the amount-matching pass-through the code computed — it is 'rare payment format plus novel counterparty on an otherwise rigidly routine account'. The bench's own known-limit note ('every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH') makes this directly recoverable, but the models' reasons show none of them used it.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The dominant visual feature of the neighborhood is two perfectly rigid recurring-payment streams (744.68/167.67 and 3569.09/12945.86 repeated for 10 days), and models split into two errors: most (claude, gpt, grok) treated the repetition as innocent standing orders and dismissed the pass-through list because amounts didn't reconcile, throwing away T1909/T2432 with it; the minority (mistral, kimi, glm) flagged the repetition itself as structuring and missed or diluted the actual labeled ACH transfers among 17-35 flagged ids. Both errors come from scoring the loud structural pattern (fixed-amount repeats) instead of the quiet deviant one (three ACH transfers to/from new counterparties on the hub).
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'Before judging, identify which transfers break the neighborhood's routine: transfers on a payment format or rail that is rare in this neighborhood, or that connect an account to a counterparty it touches only once, are higher-signal than high-volume repetition. In this data set, laundering transfers are disproportionately ACH even when most traffic is cheque or card.'
answer.system_fix: Add two code facts: (1) per-account 'novel counterparty' list — transfers to/from accounts the sender touches only once in the window (this isolates T1230, T1909, T2432 immediately); (2) format-rarity flag — transfers whose payment format is rare within the neighborhood or rare for that account. Also stop emitting amount-mismatched pass-through pairs as 'matches' (the 7 pairs here, all anchored on one 4917.74 inflow against unmatched outflows, actively baited both the false-positive and the dismissive false-negative runs); only list pass-throughs when the onward amount is within ~10% of the inbound.
answer.risk_of_fix: Flagging rare-format and novel-counterparty transfers will raise false positives on ordinary one-off payments (e.g. T0285, T2514 here would also be flagged), and hardening the pass-through amount threshold could hide genuine chains where the launderer changes amounts; on net this trades a few precise one-off alerts for catching this class, but it needs monitoring on slices where ACH is the dominant format, where the format tell is useless.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled transfer is T0714 (809305B70 -> 8093070F0, 276.29 ACH). It sits inside the 10-minute ACH burst T0713/T0714/T0717 into 8093070F0, and nothing in the rows singles it out from its two neighbors. T0713 (2628.27) and T0717 (4902.06) are the same format, bank and time window but are not labeled. The data can point to the burst as a place to look. It cannot say which of the three ACH rows, or whether any, is the laundering transfer. The labeled amount is the smallest of the three and 809305B70 has other activity (a 16310.27 ACH out at T2348, and recurring cheques), but those are weak cues, not proof.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Roughly half the runs saw the burst and either dismissed it as thin, with no onward flow and dissimilar amounts, or flagged all three ACH rows. That scores a hit on T0714 but is wrong on two of three ids. The structural truth is a lone transfer, so the burst is a decoy: the ring has no fan-in shape, and the three-sender fan-in reading is an artifact of the neighborhood sampling. The v4 and v5 confidence rules turned a correct low-confidence ring call into 'ordinary', and the models that saw mismatched pass-through amounts or recurring payments concluded nothing was there.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Every labeled laundering transfer in this slice is ACH. If the only non-routine activity is ACH rows among recurring cheque and credit-card traffic, a lone suspicious transfer is possible: name pattern lone and list only the single most anomalous ACH id, not the whole burst.' Remove or soften the rule that low-confidence ring calls become ordinary.
answer.system_fix: Add a second pass that, when the verdict is ordinary or low-confidence, ranks ACH transfers by anomaly (not part of a repeated fixed-amount series, one-off pair, unusual counterparty) and surfaces the top one as a 'lone candidate' for review. Do not auto-downgrade low-confidence calls to ordinary. Score the burst as three candidates rather than a fan-in ring.
answer.risk_of_fix: More false alarms: every one-off ACH in ordinary neighborhoods becomes a candidate. The top-one cap bounds the damage, but precision on ordinary neighborhoods will drop. The ACH-only tell also holds only on this synthetic slice and would not transfer to real data. Picking one of three burst rows is close to a coin flip, so expect about a third precision on the id.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0714 is one of only four ACH transfers, but the rows provide no transfer-specific evidence that distinguishes it as laundering. Its ten-minute arrival alongside T0713 and T0717 identifies a burst, not why only T0714 is labeled. T2348 occurs a week after T0713 and cannot explain that earlier payment as a time-ordered chain.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models that called the neighborhood ordinary missed the labeled transfer because a lone labeled payment need not form a visible scheme. Models that found the ACH fan-in included T0714 but also flagged the unlabeled T0713 and T0717; the burst cannot recover the dataset's one-transfer boundary.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "For a lone pattern, do not assign laundering to an individual transfer based only on its payment format or membership in a burst; if no transfer-specific evidence separates it from its neighbors, say its labeled identity is not recoverable from these rows."
answer.system_fix: If identification of lone labeled transfers is required, supply independently verified transaction-level evidence or labels. No rule computed from this neighborhood can reliably select T0714 alone.
answer.risk_of_fix: The abstention rule may leave genuine lone transfers undetected; flagging every ACH or every member of the burst instead would create false alarms on T0713, T0717, and potentially T2348.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair is a two-hop fragment, not an amount-conserving flow. T1422 (2022/09/05 12:33, 80AD40250→808C30740, 12228.11 UK Pound, ACH) is 80AD40250's only send that is not the repeated 41915.85 Australian Dollar cheque to 80B2988C0 (T0258, T0936, T1424, T1579, T1824, T2137). T1870 (2022/09/07 06:13, 808C30740→8100920E0, 50878.02 Shekel, ACH) is 808C30740's only outbound, 41.7h later, and the only edge from the UK Pound collector into the Shekel hub. Those two ids are the only path joining the three otherwise separate currency clusters. Same funds cannot be shown: currencies differ and 12228.11 does not equal 50878.02. The other 52 rows are recurring same-amount corridors (including 10 other ACH rows) plus three identical unlabeled 32922640.04 Shekel cash deposits (T0433, T2226, T2535). The pass-through facts never surface T1422→T1870; they pair T1870 with tiny recurring inflows T1359 and T1361.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Early runs called a ring but flagged the unlabeled 32.9M cash fan-out around 8100920E0 (haiku, deepseek, mistral, glm, luna) and missed the bridge, or buried T1422 and T1870 in dozens of flags (kimi). Once the prompt and facts required a directed loop, a multi-counterparty burst, or a pass-through that moves nearly the whole amount in the same currency, later runs (sonnet v2–v5, sol v2–v5, grok v2) correctly rejected that cash corridor and then called the neighborhood ordinary, dropping the only true chain. sol v1 had already named exactly T1422 and T1870 from the raw rows as the two-hop cross-currency route that stands out from repeated payments; the amount-conservation tests erased that hit.
answer.prompt_fix: Replace any rule that a chain must move nearly the whole incoming amount in the same currency with: a chain may be a two-transfer fragment of a longer stack, and the two amounts and currencies need not match; flag only the pair where one transfer is an account's sole payment outside its repeated same-counterparty, same-amount corridor and the other is the middle account's only outbound (T1422 then T1870). Do not treat repeated identical amounts on a single corridor as a scheme, including T0433, T2226 and T2535, and do not flag the recurring inflows that only share the middle account.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact, sole bridges: each account's only outbound, plus any inbound that is the sender's only payment outside a repeated same-amount corridor, joined if within 48 hours even when currency and amount differ, and always emit that pair (T1422–T1870, 41.7h, UK Pound to Shekel) instead of truncating the pass-through list and pairing T1870 with T1359/T1361. Do not add an ACH filter; 10 of 12 ACH rows here are not labeled.
answer.risk_of_fix: A genuine one-off payment into an account that later makes its only onward payment, in a different currency and amount, would be flagged even if the funds are unrelated. If 'only payment outside the corridor' is applied loosely, ordinary new beneficiaries of busy accounts are pulled in.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Three of the four ACH transfers are the labeled ids and center on account 80AA72BA0: T1909 is an ACH AUD 4917.74 inflow from 8018514B0; T1230 is an ACH AUD 198.76 outflow to 80AA72E10; T2432 is an ACH USD 3593.22 outflow to 8022AF930. The fourth ACH, T0285 (8022AF930→8022BACE0), does not touch 80AA72BA0 and is unlabeled. Temporally T1230 precedes T1909, so the labeled ring is a hub/star around 80AA72BA0 rather than a strict A→B→C pass-through. The two high-volume streams that dominate the neighborhood are entirely cheque/credit-card, e.g. T0357/T0367/T0655/T0658 and T0857/T0859/T1105/T1107.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models weighted graph motifs and the dominant recurring cheque/card pairs, which appeared either ordinary or like structuring, and largely ignored payment format. The tiny ACH set containing the labels was therefore dismissed as weak or buried among false alarms; models that flagged many ids often flagged the unlabeled recurring cheque/card transfers to 80AD21FA0 instead.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'In this data set the main-slice laundering transfers are ACH. Before judging recurring cheque/card flows, list the ACH transfers and, if a small ACH set is incident to a single busy account, especially one sending to multiple other accounts, treat that ACH set as the scheme and flag those ids.'
answer.system_fix: Compute and show the ACH subgraph explicitly: for each account, ACH in/out counts and the connected ACH component, placing it above the pass-through/burst summary so rare-format edges are not crowded out by cheque/card volume.
answer.risk_of_fix: It would over-flag isolated ACH payments such as T0285 unless constrained to ACH edges incident to a multi-counterparty hub. More generally, 'ACH = laundering' is a synthetic-data tell and will not transfer to real traffic without additional features.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The single labeled transfer T0714 (276.29 ACH from 809305B70 to 8093070F0, 2022/09/02 05:08) is structurally indistinguishable from its unlabeled neighbors. It sits inside the 10-minute burst T0713/T0714/T0717 into 8093070F0, but T0713 and T0717 are the same pattern (one-off ACH from a distinct sender, dissimilar amount) and are not labeled. Its sender 809305B70's other nine transfers are the recurring 1929.27 cheques and the 16310.27 ACH T2348, none labeled; its receiver 8093070F0 never sends onward, so no downstream trace exists. The prompt's own known-limits hint ('every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH') marks 11 of 28 rows as ACH candidates and does not single out T0714.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Because the truth is a single labeled transfer with no unique structure, the task degenerated into whether the 3-transfer burst T0713/T0714/T0717 looks like a fan-in: models that called 'ring' flagged exactly that burst (1 of 3 labeled, by luck), and models that called 'ordinary' reasonably noted there is no loop, no amount-matched chain, and no onward movement. The 'lone' pattern was in the scheme list but the prompt never told models that a lone ring can look like an ordinary transfer inside an innocent-looking burst, so every model searched for multi-row structure that does not exist here.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the scheme definitions: 'lone: exactly one suspicious transfer, which may have NO distinguishing structure of its own — it can be an unremarkable row sitting inside a burst or recurring series; if the neighborhood is otherwise ordinary but one transfer is an outlier (e.g., the only ACH from a sender whose other payments are all cheques, or the smallest/odd-amount member of a burst), name lone and list that single id rather than the whole burst.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact for within-burst and within-account outlier detection: for each burst, rank members by deviation from the sender's own history (T0714 is the only ACH 809305B70 ever sent to 8093070F0; its amount 276.29 is far below the sender's 1929.27/16310.27 norms), and surface 'most anomalous single transfer' as an explicit fact. That gives models a concrete candidate for lone verdicts instead of all-or-nothing burst flags.
answer.risk_of_fix: Explicitly inviting single-transfer 'lone' verdicts will raise false positives: models may start naming one 'anomalous' row in every ordinary neighborhood (e.g., the 16310.27 T2348 here, or any odd-amount bill payment), converting clean ordinary calls into accusations against real customers.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled laundering transfer is T0714, a 276.29 Canadian Dollar ACH from 809305B70 to 8093070F0 on 2022/09/02 05:08. The computed facts narrow the candidates only to the four ACH rows: T0713, T0714, T0717, and T2348, because every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. T0714 sits inside the single computed burst: T0713, T0714, and T0717 are three ACH payments from three distinct accounts into 8093070F0 within 10 minutes. But no row-level feature separates T0714 from T0713 and T0717: all three are one-off ACH receipts by 8093070F0 with no onward movement, and their amounts differ widely (2628.27, 276.29, 4902.06). T0714's sender 809305B70 is otherwise active in recurring 1929.27 cheques to 809560410 and pass-through pairs, but those companion rows are not labeled. Thus the data can narrow suspicion to the ACH burst, but cannot recover the exact single-row label.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models anchored on visible multi-transfer patterns: the ten-minute fan-in looked either like ordinary batch receipts because there was no onward flow and unequal amounts, or like a complete three-transfer ring, so they either returned ordinary or flagged T0713/T0714/T0717 together. No model could justify isolating T0714 alone, because the rows contain no signal for IBM's single-row label beyond ACH format and burst membership, and the dominating recurring cheque/credit-card traffic distracted attention from the one labeled ACH.
answer.prompt_fix: Add this rule to the prompt: 'A single ACH transfer can be a laundering ring in this data. If a short ACH burst from distinct accounts arrives at one beneficiary, report each ACH leg as a fan-in even if there is no onward movement and amounts differ; do not let recurring cheque/credit-card series turn that ACH burst into ordinary.'

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The two labeled transfers are T1671 (800055A70 -> 800122600, 14,148.02 EUR, ACH, 2022-09-06 11:32) and T2179 (800122600 -> 800177290, 13,278.65 EUR, ACH, 2022-09-08 12:55). answer.why_the_models_failed: The code's pass-through facts listed only pairs anchored on 8000677F0's large inflows (T0341, T0344) against small outflows, so the amount-matched pair T1671/T2179 never appeared in the facts and was buried under 18 mismatched pairs. Models then either read the hub as fan-out and flagged 8-31 ids that missed or diluted the two real rows, or concluded 'ordinary' because outflows were small relative to the 395k inflow. Only sonnet-5-5 v1 on raw rows spotted the 94% pass-through, and later models, even gpt-6-sol, which noticed T1671 and T2179 as a possible two-hop path, dismissed it because amounts and timing 'alone do not establish' a scheme.
answer.prompt_fix: Replace the guidance on pass-through with: 'A pass-through counts when an outflow is within about 10% of one specific inflow to the same account within 72 hours. Compare each outflow only with inflows of similar size, ignore large unrelated inflows, and when you find such a matched pair, report exactly those two transfer ids as a chain rather than the whole hub.' Optionally add: 'Among these rows, ACH transfers between different accounts deserve the closest look.'

Also give the ACH-only subgraph as a separate fact. As a second pass, ask the model to judge only the top matched pair instead of the whole neighborhood.

It will also flag only two-transfer chains and may not extend to the longer IBM stack.
