answer.evidence_in_the_data: The ground truth is a 'lone' ring: exactly one labeled transfer, T0290. Nothing in the rows or computed facts singles T0290 out from T0291 and T0292 — all three are ACH inflows to 80C988190 within 11 minutes from three different banks, with amounts 1657.88 / 2479.52 / 3194.19. The only bench-level tells are the stated known limits: every labeled transfer in the main slice is ACH (which excludes the 14 cheque/credit-card rows from 8034A5880), and a lone ring is a single labeled transfer. So the data can narrow the answer to the set {T0290, T0291, T0292} but cannot pick T0290 over its two neighbors; the 14 recurring fixed-amount transfers are structurally ordinary (repeated 126.02/65.12 pairs, near-daily cadence, classic recurring payments).
answer.why_the_models_failed: The 11-minute three-sender ACH burst (T0290-T0292) looks exactly like the 'fan-in' pattern the prompt names, so models that flagged anything flagged all three — but the truth is a lone transfer, so any flag beyond one id is a wrong accusation, and no model could justify picking T0290 specifically. Meanwhile several models (mistral v1/v2, kimi, glm v2, deepseek v2, gpt-6-luna) also swept in the 14 recurring cheque/card payments as 'structuring', a clear recurring-payments false positive that diluted precision further. The 'ordinary' models failed differently: they demanded onward movement (pass-through/loops) that a lone ring by definition never has, so their 'no layering' reasoning structurally guarantees missing this class.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the pattern list: 'A lone ring is a single labeled transfer hiding inside ordinary-looking traffic; it has no fan-in, loop, chain, or onward movement by definition, so absence of structure does not rule it out. If you suspect a lone ring, flag your single most suspicious transfer id — never a group — and remember that in this slice only ACH rows can be labeled.'
answer.system_fix: Add one code fact to the neighborhood summary: 'candidate lone-transfer rows: ACH transfers whose counterparties do not recur elsewhere in the neighborhood' — here that yields exactly T0290, T0291, T0292 (one-off senders, ACH), excluding the 14 recurring 8034A5880 rows. This gives models a pre-filtered shortlist to pick one from instead of either flagging the whole burst or the whole neighborhood.
answer.risk_of_fix: Prompting for a single most-suspicious id will convert some 'ordinary' verdicts into one-id guesses, adding a small false-positive cost on truly ordinary neighborhoods that contain a one-off ACH burst (like T0290-T0292 would be in a clean neighborhood), and the ACH-only hint leaks the bench's slice artifact, so the fix would not generalize to slices where labeled transfers use other formats.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The rows show the signature of standing business payments, not layering. They contain no ACH row that fits a scheme. Five identical 71020.50 cheques go 80A5D58A0 -> 80A817660 (T0672, T1192, T1430, T1566, T2724), and fixed amounts repeat on fixed routes: 20400.53 cheque x4 to 80AF80930 (T0678, T1444, T1920, T2145), 13706.74 cash x3 to 80A985FF0 (T1226, T2494, T2720), 1401.97 x2 (T0703, T1763), and 4340.06 x2 (T0390, T1924). Only two sinks exist, with no loops, no bursts and no return flow. The hub's outflows are much smaller than its inflows (about 355k in versus about 170k out), and the outgoing amounts never equal the incoming ones. Feeders such as T0401 (178.26) and T1534 (48723.11) cannot fund a 71020.50 leg. The 'within hours' timing is a product of dense repetition, since 19 pass-through pairs come from only a handful of recurring legs. The labels cannot be proven from the rows alone, since a real scheme could look like this. The absence of any ACH laundering signal and the all-cheque/cash mix point to ordinary traffic.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models treated exact amount repetition and 80A817660 forwarding money to two accounts within hours as proof of a layered chain, even though the repetition is just as consistent with scheduled payments. The 19 pass-through pairs were counted as evidence, when they are mostly the same few recurring legs matched against each other with unequal amounts. The models that said ordinary (v5 prompts, grok v2) reasoned correctly from the unmatched amounts and the lack of loops, bursts or broad fan-out, while the rest flagged 14 to 20 ids with hedged language.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Identical amounts that repeat on the same sender-receiver route at regular intervals are standing payments, not layering. Call a chain only if the amount leaving an account roughly matches what just arrived (within a few percent) and the route does not repeat. If outflows are smaller than inflows and only 1-2 counterparties recur, answer ordinary.' Also state that every labeled laundering transfer is ACH, so a neighborhood dominated by Cheque, Cash and Credit Card with only two small ACH rows (T0401, T1565) should default to ordinary.
answer.system_fix: Add code facts: (1) the number of distinct routes and how many repeat 3 or more times; (2) per pass-through pair, an amount-match ratio (out/in), with a count of pairs where the ratio is above 0.8; (3) the ACH share of rows. Collapse repeated pairs into unique routes before counting pass-through pairs, so 19 pairs become roughly 5 routes. Optionally run a second pass that only asks whether any ACH transfer is anomalous.
answer.risk_of_fix: A real layering scheme that reuses fixed amounts on repeating routes, or one that splits a deposit into smaller equal parts, would be dismissed. The ACH-only hint would miss any laundering outside this synthetic slice, and the amount-match rule would miss structured splits where outflows sum to the inflow.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: In the main slice, 18 of these 20 transfers cannot be labeled laundering because they are not ACH. The two ACH rows, T0401 and T1565, have no distinctive evidence here that establishes their ordinary labels. The repeated T0672/T1192/T1430/T1566/T2724 receipts and fixed payments such as T0678/T1444/T1920/T2145 form recurring routes, but the listed 48-hour pairs establish timing, not that particular incoming funds were forwarded. The absence of labeled transfers within 120 minutes of these accounts is not recoverable from this neighborhood alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models treated identical amounts on fixed routes and nearby onward payments as proof of a laundering chain, despite only two downstream recipients and no demonstrated tracing of funds. Some also promoted every transfer on the connected path into the ring; the v5 ordinary verdicts and grok v2 avoided that inference.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'For this main-slice task, exclude non-ACH rows from any proposed labeled scheme; repeated payments to fixed counterparties and time-only pass-through pairs do not by themselves establish laundering, so call the neighborhood ordinary unless an eligible ACH row has additional scheme-specific evidence.'
answer.system_fix: Before model review, mark label-eligible rows using the known main-slice ACH constraint and report amount-aware, non-overlapping candidate flows separately from all time-only pass-through pairs. Here that leaves only T0401 and T1565 eligible, neither supported by the apparent recurring-payment chain.
answer.risk_of_fix: An ACH-labeled lone transfer or short chain could be missed when its distinguishing evidence lies outside the neighborhood. The ACH gate must not be applied to another slice or dataset without verifying that its labels follow the same rule.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The real chain is visible in the rows: T1671 (800055A70 -> 800122600, 14,148.02 EUR, ACH, 2022/09/06 11:32) followed by T2179 (800122600 -> 800177290, 13,278.65 EUR, ACH, 2022/09/08 12:55), i.e. ~94% of the money passed on within ~49 hours, both ACH, both one-off amounts that never recur. What buries it: the computed 'pass-through pairs' fact lists 10 of 18 pairs and every listed one pairs a huge inflow (91k/144k from 8000677F0) with a tiny outflow (79.77, 295.66...), teaching models that 'pass-through here means amount mismatch'. The T1671->T2179 pair is not even shown in the fact list despite being the only near-amount-conserving pair. The two much larger 8000677F0 inflows (T0341, T0344, T2668) are decoys with no matching outflow, and models anchored on them.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models were trained by the fact block to test pass-through as 'did the big money move onward?', and since the 91k/144k inflows only exit as small payments, most concluded 'no scheme' (openai, xai, sonnet v2+). The one real chain, T1671->T2179, conserves ~94% of a mid-size amount rather than being the largest flow, so it ranked below the decoy inflows in attention. Models that did flag rings (mistral, kimi, deepseek v2) over-flagged the fan-out and recurring payments instead. Only sonnet v1, reasoning over raw rows without the misleading fact list, isolated exactly T1671/T2179.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A chain can be a mid-sized transfer, not the largest one: check every pass-through pair for amount conservation (outflow >= ~70% of a single recent inflow). A near-whole pass-through of a moderate amount is stronger evidence of layering than a large inflow that only leaks out in small pieces.'
answer.system_fix: Change the pass-through fact: for each pair, compute and sort by amount ratio (outflow / matched inflow), show all pairs not just the first 10, and surface a dedicated fact 'near-whole forwardings (outflow >= 70% of inflow within 72h)' — this would list 800055A70 -> 800122600 -> 800177290 (T1671, T2179, ratio 0.94) at the top and demote the 8000677F0 big-in/small-out pairs.
answer.risk_of_fix: Highlighting amount-conserving pairs will occasionally flag ordinary two-hop flows (e.g. a business receiving an invoice payment and paying a similar-sized supplier bill days later), so some ordinary neighborhoods with one coincidental ratio-0.9 pair will get flagged; the 70% threshold and requiring a single matched inflow (not an aggregate) keeps this rare.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1671 sends 14,148.02 EUR by ACH from 800055A70 to 800122600 on 2022-09-06 11:32; T2179 sends 13,278.65 EUR by ACH from 800122600 to 800177290 on 2022-09-08 12:55. That is 93.9% of T1671 passed onward in the same currency and payment format, a two-hop chain. The code facts missed this pair because the gap is 49.4 hours, just over the 48-hour pass-through threshold. The larger cheque inflows from 8000677F0 to 800122600 (T0341, T0344, T2668) are a red herring and do not amount-match the small outflows.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v2+ facts listed pass-through pairs only from the 8000677F0 inflows because T1671->T2179 was just beyond the 48-hour window, so the true chain never appeared as a computed pair. Models then compared 800122600's aggregate inflows (~395k) with its ~31k outflows and concluded the hub was not forwarding money, treating T2179 as just one small outflow; raw-row v1 models that did see the pair often buried it among 20+ fan-out false positives.
answer.prompt_fix: A suspicious chain can be as short as two transfers: if an account receives a large same-currency payment and within 96 hours sends at least 80% of that amount onward to a different account in the same currency and format, flag both transfers as a chain even if the account has unrelated large inflows or many small outflows.
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact for amount-matched onward pairs: for each incoming transfer, search up to 96 hours ahead for an outgoing transfer from the same account in the same currency and payment format whose amount is 80-120% of the incoming amount. This would surface T1671-T2179; the existing 48-hour pass-through list missed it.
answer.risk_of_fix: The wider 96-hour window and amount-ratio test will catch ordinary businesses that receive a large payment and later make a similar-sized legitimate payment, generating more false alerts. It should be limited to large ACH/EUR flows and probably followed by a second review rather than auto-alerting.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing positively labels this ordinary, but the structure argues against layering: 80A817660 receives 5 x 71,020.50 (T0672, T1192, T1430, T1566, T2724) yet sends out only small fixed amounts (20,400.53 x4 to 80AF80930: T0678, T1444, T1920, T2145; 13,706.74 cash x3 to 80A985FF0: T1226, T2494, T2720), retaining most of what arrives — the opposite of pass-through. Outgoing amounts never match incoming ones, there are 0 loops, 0 bursts, only 2 downstream recipients, and the identical cent-level amounts recur on a regular multi-day cadence (every ~1-3 days over 9 days), which reads as standing/scheduled payments (rent, payroll, supplier invoices), not structuring. The bench hint that every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH also cuts against a ring here: the repeated legs are Cheque/Cash (T0672 etc.), with only T0401 and T1565 being ACH and neither connected to anything labeled.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models treated 'repeated identical amounts + pass-through pairs within 48h' as a layering signature, without checking amount conservation: a real pass-through moves roughly what it receives, while 80A817660 pays out ~20-40% of each inbound 71,020.50 and keeps the rest. The code fact '19 pass-through pairs' actively misled them — pairing any inbound with any outbound within 48h manufactures 'layering' out of an account that simply has frequent traffic both ways. v5 (and grok v2) got it right only because a tighter rule forced them to weigh loops/bursts/fan-out degree and amount mismatch over the cloned-amount pattern.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'Recurring identical amounts between the same two accounts on a regular cadence are the hallmark of standing business payments (rent, payroll, retainers), not layering; before calling a chain or pass-through, check amount conservation — if the middle account retains most of what it receives and sends out smaller fixed amounts to few recipients, that is ordinary scheduled traffic, not forwarding.'
answer.system_fix: Change the pass-through-pair fact: require the outbound amount to be within ~15% of the inbound amount (or require near-total onward movement of funds within the window) before listing a pair, and add a per-account 'retention ratio' (total out / total in) plus a 'recurrence cadence' fact (same amount, same counterparty, >=3 times on a regular interval) so recurring standing payments are surfaced as such rather than as 19 raw pass-through pairs.
answer.risk_of_fix: A strict amount-matching pass-through filter would miss real layering that skims a fee or splits amounts before forwarding, and a retention-ratio fact could be gamed by rings that forward everything; the 'recurring cadence = ordinary' hint could also cause true installments-based structuring to be waved through if applied without the conservation check.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The rows show fixed recurring standing payments, not a laundering chain. 80A5D58A0 sends 80A817660 the same 71,020.50 AUD cheque five times on 2022-09-02, 09-04, 09-05, 09-06 and 09-10 (T0672, T1192, T1430, T1566, T2724), and 80A817660 sends recurring fixed amounts to only two recipients: 20,400.53 cheque to 80AF80930 (T0678, T1444, T1920, T2145), 13,706.74 cash to 80A985FF0 (T1226, T2494, T2720), 1,401.97 cheque (T0703, T1763), and 4,340.06 credit card (T0390, T1924). These fixed-amount, repeating counterparty pairs are spaced days apart, with 0 directed loops, 0 bursts, and only two distinct onward recipients. The incoming 71,020.50 is not split into matching outgoing legs: after T0672, for example, outflows T0678 (20,400.53) and T0703 (1,401.97) total only 21,802.50, so most is retained rather than passed through. The bench note that every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH is also decisive: the allegedly suspicious repeated amounts are Cheque/Cash/Credit Card, while the only ACH rows are small one-offs T0401 and T1565 outside the repeated pattern.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models treated repeated identical amounts and 'money arrives and leaves within 48h' as layering, though fixed recurring payments between the same two accounts over several days are the signature of standing orders. They also ignored the format rule they were given: in this main slice all labeled laundering is ACH, and the repeated Cheque/Cash/Credit Card legs do not meet that tell. The v5/tighter runs and a few v2 runs show the correction already works by requiring conserved outflow or broader fan-out before calling a ring.
answer.prompt_fix: Add this rule to the prompt: 'Repeated identical amounts between the same two accounts, especially spaced days apart and not in ACH, are ordinary standing payments unless outgoing transfers rapidly split the incoming amount across three or more distinct accounts and sum near the incoming amount. In this main slice all labeled laundering is ACH, so treat non-ACH recurrence as ordinary by default.'
answer.system_fix: Replace the pass-through-pair fact with a recurring-payment fact: group identical (from_account, to_account, amount, payment_format) rows and report count plus median interval; require either three or more distinct recipients or a conserved sum before emitting a chain/pass-through signal.
answer.risk_of_fix: It will overweight the synthetic ACH-only artifact and may miss real laundering done through cheque, cash, credit card, or tight two-account layering in other slices or real data.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled row is T1126 (811334860 -> 8113348B0, 9884.18 Shekel, ACH, 2022/09/03 10:14). It is one of only 3 ACH rows. The other ACH row, T0767 (147088.38), is large and unlabeled. T1126 is the sole transfer from 811334860, which has no other history, and its amount is just under 10,000. The bench note says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. That narrows the candidates to T0767 and T1126, and T1126 is the better pick because of the near-threshold amount and the one-off sender. The other 16 rows, including the 14 repeated 1935.12 and 1346.02 rows from 810C151B0 and the large cheque T0768, show no laundering structure. Nothing in the rows proves that T1126 is laundering; the label is IBM's own and only weakly visible. The two-way pick between T1126 and T0767 cannot be settled with certainty from the data.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The neighborhood has a lone labeled transfer buried in a busy collector account. Models that said ring flagged all 17 rows as a fan-in, so they hit T1126 but with 16 false rows. Models that said ordinary dismissed the 14 recurring payments and the 3-sender convergence, and so missed T1126 as well. Nobody isolated a single row, because the prompt framing steers toward topology (fan-in, loops, pass-through) and the code facts have no per-transfer signal for a lone ACH row.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "A 'lone' ring is a single transfer. If there is no topology but exactly one row stands out (an ACH transfer just under a round reporting threshold from a sender with no other history), return pattern lone and list only that id. Never list a recurring sender's repeated fixed-amount rows, and do not treat many inbound rows to one account as a scheme unless there are 3+ distinct senders within a short window."
answer.system_fix: Add per-transfer code facts: flag ACH rows, flag amounts within 5% below 10,000, and flag senders with exactly one transfer in the neighborhood. Add a recurring-payment fact that marks senders repeating identical amounts 5+ times so that those rows are excluded from candidates. Score a single-row candidate in a second pass instead of an all-or-nothing neighborhood verdict.
answer.risk_of_fix: Many ordinary one-off ACH payments sit near 10k, so the lone rule would raise false alarms on a wider data set, and naming T1126 rather than T0767 is a guess. The exclusion of recurring senders would also hide a real structuring ring made of repeated fixed amounts.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only near-conserving path is T1671 (800055A70 to 800122600, 14148.02 Euro, ACH, 2022/09/06 11:32) then T2179 (800122600 to 800177290, 13278.65 Euro, ACH, 2022/09/08 12:55): 93.9% retained, 49.4 hours later, just outside the 48-hour pass-through list. No third hop is in this neighborhood (800177290 only sends recurring small amounts such as 348.40 and 282.01), and the large 8000677F0 credits T0341, T0344 and T2668 are never forwarded at similar size. The longer stack is cut off, so the ring is only this two-hop fragment.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The 48-hour fact list omitted T1671 to T2179 and instead listed 18 amount-mismatched pairs through 800122600, so v2 and later models either dismissed every pass-through as a timing coincidence or called the hub a fan-out and flagged the wrong ids. Models that required a cycle, a burst, an exact amount match, or a sub-48-hour window returned ordinary (sonnet v2 through v5, gpt-6, grok), even when gpt-6-sol v1 had already noticed T1671 and T2179. Only sonnet v1, on raw rows, named the chain and exactly those two ids.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: A chain needs only two hops: flag the ids when an account receives amount X and within 72 hours pays a different account 85 to 100 percent of X in the same currency, even with no cycle, burst, third hop, or entry in the 48-hour pass-through list. Do not treat a large inflow followed only by much smaller payments as a scheme.
answer.system_fix: Replace the any-amount 48-hour pass-through list with a near-conserving fact: same currency, outbound/inbound in [0.85, 1.05], window 72 hours. On these rows that emits only T1671 then T2179 and drops the 18 mismatched pairs through 800122600.
answer.risk_of_fix: Legitimate similar-sized payments through an intermediary inside 72 hours (invoice then payout, internal reallocation) would be flagged; the 85-100 percent band limits that but does not remove it.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The bench's known ACH-only label constraint narrows the candidates to T0767 and T1126. T1126 is the sole transfer from 811334860 and is not part of the repeated payments or the large, three-minute T0767–T0768 pair. Those distinctions make it a candidate for a lone pattern, but no field establishes why T1126, rather than T0767, has IBM's laundering label. Its 9,884.18 Shekel amount does not establish proximity to any applicable reporting threshold.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models that returned ordinary treated the absence of loops, pass-through, onward movement, and a strong fan-in as grounds to dismiss every transfer, missing the possibility of a single labeled row. Models that returned fan-in flagged all 17 transfers because they shared a recipient, capturing T1126 only by also accusing 16 unlabeled rows.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Check each eligible transfer for a possible lone pattern separately from network patterns, but do not call a transfer laundering solely because it is ACH, isolated, or near an assumed threshold; if the rows cannot distinguish it from ordinary activity, say so."
answer.system_fix: Add an ACH-candidate second pass that seeks independent account-history or risk evidence before a positive lone-transfer verdict. With only these 17 rows, it should leave T1126 unresolved rather than automatically flag it.
answer.risk_of_fix: Automatically flagging isolated ACH receipts would create false alarms on ordinary one-off payments; requiring independent evidence may still miss T1126 when that evidence is unavailable.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing structural singles out T1126: the neighborhood is a pure collector (8113348B0 receives 17, sends 0) with no loops, chains, or pass-through, which is why the structural reading is 'lone'. The only recoverable tells are weak and indirect: T1126 is an ACH for 9,884.18 — just under the 10,000 reporting threshold — and the bench's own hint says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. T1126 is one of only two ACH rows (the other is T0767, 147,088.38), so an ACH-plus-just-under-threshold rule would nominate T1126 but also drag in T0767. The sender 811334860 appears exactly once and is otherwise indistinguishable from the other two senders. Beyond that, the label is not recoverable from these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models split into two failure modes, both wrong about the same truth. The 'ring/fan-in' callers (haiku, deepseek, kimi, glm, grok v2, mistral v2) over-read a pure one-way collection as a scheme and flagged all 17 rows — 16 of them benign recurring payments — catching T1126 only by accident. The 'ordinary' callers (sonnet, gpt-6-sol, gpt-6-luna v2) correctly reasoned that there is no fan-in, loop, or pass-through structure, but then had no mechanism to surface a single suspicious transfer, so the lone labeled row T1126 went unflagged. The prompt's scheme taxonomy forces a structural verdict and gives no sanctioned way to say 'mostly ordinary, but flag T1126'.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A neighborhood can be structurally ordinary yet still contain a lone suspicious transfer. If you verdict ordinary, separately list any individual transfer that is anomalous on its own — e.g. a one-off ACH just under a round reporting threshold (like 10,000) from an account that appears only once — and flag only those ids, not the whole neighborhood.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed per-transfer fact: a 'first-and-only-seen sender' flag and a 'just-under-threshold' flag (amount within 2% below 10,000), plus an ACH indicator surfaced explicitly per row; then run a cheap second pass that, when the structural verdict is ordinary, asks only about rows carrying two or more of these flags. Here that isolates T1126 (ACH, 9,884.18, sender seen once) without touching the recurring 810C151B0 payments.
answer.risk_of_fix: The just-under-10k-plus-ACH rule will also flag T0767-type rows in other neighborhoods and any legitimate near-threshold payroll or rent ACH, adding a small stream of single-transfer false positives; and explicitly telling models the main-slice-is-ACH hint invites them to over-weight payment format, which the v2x runs show is not itself decisive.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The rows show a single account pair, 80A3DE9A0 to 80A4A6D80, sending the same four amounts (34180.84 Cheque, 28735.64 Credit Card, 19908.12 ACH, 12638.22 Cash) in T0785/T0790/T0794/T0796 on 09/02 and again in T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389 on 09/09. That is one counterparty, with no loop, no fan-out and no fan-in, so there is no multi-account structure. The inflows T2251 (635.64) and T2252 (3359.48) are a small fraction of the roughly 95k that goes out, so the eight 'pass-through' pairs are unsupported. The only bench rule that points to ordinary traffic is that every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. Here only T0794 and T2384 are ACH, and each is a mid-sized member of a mixed-format batch. That makes the batches unlikely to be labeled, but it is circumstantial. The data cannot prove that the repeat is a legitimate payment run. Exact replay of identical amounts and formats a week apart is weakly consistent with either scheduled settlement or scripted structuring. The ground truth is therefore only partly recoverable from the rows themselves.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models treated exact amount-and-format repetition across two tight bursts as structuring, even though it involves a single sender and a single recipient with no layering. The v2 facts (four bursts, eight pass-through pairs) added to the alarm, and some models flagged 10 ids by including T2251/T2252. Models that said ordinary read the repeat as a scheduled payment run, which is the better reading, but nothing in the prompt told them that mixed-format bursts are inconsistent with this bench's labeled laundering.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Repeated identical amounts between one sender and one recipient, even in bursts and across several payment formats, are a recurring payment run, not a scheme, unless a loop, a fan-out/fan-in to three or more accounts, or a chain with matching amounts is also present. In this bench, labeled laundering transfers are ACH only, so a batch that is mostly Cheque, Credit Card or Cash is evidence for ordinary traffic.' Also remove the loose 'other' option as a way to flag a single-pair repeat.
answer.system_fix: Change the pass-through fact so it only reports a pair when the outgoing amount is within about 20 percent of the incoming amount, or when the outflow is at most the inflow. This case would drop all eight pairs, since 635.64 and 3359.48 against 12k to 34k do not match. Add a fact 'distinct counterparties per burst' and a fact 'share of ACH rows in a candidate ring', and require a burst to have at least 3 distinct counterparties before it is labeled a burst. Add a repeat-schedule fact that detects the same amount set recurring at an interval, so it can be shown as a recurring-payment signal.
answer.risk_of_fix: A real structuring scheme that is replayed between one pair of accounts, or one that uses ACH only, would be dismissed. A pass-through detector with an amount-match threshold would miss layering in which money is split or fees are skimmed. The ACH-only rule would also suppress a genuine non-ACH scheme if the bench labels ever changed.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Ordinary standing payments, not a scheme. Fixed routes repeat non-round cent amounts over days: 71020.50 cheque 80A5D58A0→80A817660 five times (T0672, T1192, T1430, T1566, T2724); 20400.53 cheque 80A817660→80AF80930 four times (T0678, T1444, T1920, T2145); 13706.74 cash to 80A985FF0 three times (T1226, T2494, T2720); 4340.06 twice (T0390, T1924); 1401.97 twice (T0703, T1763). Facts show 0 loops and 0 bursts, and the hub pays only two counterparties. Amounts do not pass through: credits into 80A5D58A0 (T0401 178.26, T1547 819.21, T1534 48723.11) cannot fund five 71020.50 cheques; 80A817660 receives ~360926.79 and sends ~134206.40, so it keeps most of the money; onward legs are not ~71020.50. T0390 leaves before any inflow in the slice; T2724 arrives with no later outflow. The 19 pass-through pairs are a 48-hour window over two independent recurring streams (e.g. T0401 178.26 paired with T0672 71020.50).
answer.why_the_models_failed: Twenty-two of twenty-six runs called a ring because five identical 71020.50 cheques plus repeated 20400.53 and 13706.74 outflows looked like layering, and v2+ runs treated the 19 amount-blind pass-through pairs as proof the funds moved on. Those pairs do not reconcile, there is no loop or burst, and only two outbound counterparties, so the repeats are standing payments. v1 models made the same call from the raw rows, so the failure is the recurring-amount heuristic, not only the pass-through fact.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: Repeated identical amounts on a fixed from-account to to-account route, especially non-round amounts with cents, are standing payments and are not a chain, fan-out, or pass-through unless an onward leg carries nearly the same amount within a few hours or the money returns to an earlier account.
answer.system_fix: Stop emitting pass-through pairs whose outbound amount is not within a small fee of the inbound amount (drop pairs such as T0401 178.26 with T0672 71020.50); report only amount-matched pass-throughs, plus each account's inflow total, outflow total, and retention ratio.
answer.risk_of_fix: Would miss a real scheme hidden in many identical recurring payments, or one that splits a credit into several much smaller debits so no single onward leg matches. It would not by itself clear a one-shot chain whose onward amount nearly matches the inbound amount.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1126 is the only transfer from account 811334860, the only ACH transfer under 10,000 (9,884.18 Shekel, 98.84% of a 10,000 reporting threshold), and it lands in 8113348B0, the account that otherwise receives recurring fixed-amount cash/cheque payments plus two much larger ACH/cheque transfers. T1126's format and just-under-threshold amount mark it as the lone suspicious transfer; the other 16 rows either repeat non-ACH fixed amounts or are large one-off credits.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models read the whole neighborhood as a fan-in and either flagged all 17 rows or cleared all 17 because there was no onward flow, cycle or pass-through. T1126 was treated as one more inbound transfer rather than as the lone suspicious ACH, and none of the 26 runs returned exactly T1126.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A scheme may be a single lone transfer: if an account receives an ACH payment just below a common reporting threshold (9,000-10,000) from a sender with no other transfers in the neighborhood, return pattern lone and list exactly that transfer id, even when the rest of the neighborhood looks like ordinary recurring or fan-in traffic.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact per row `near_threshold_ach` (payment_format == 'ACH' and amount between 9,000 and 10,000) and require the model to evaluate lone candidates before deciding ordinary when this fact is present.
answer.risk_of_fix: This could newly flag legitimate ACH payments that happen to be just below 10,000, especially businesses or rent/loan payments made by ACH from an occasional payer; without account history it cannot distinguish a real structuring payment from an innocent below-threshold transfer.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0785/T0790/T0794/T0796 and T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389 are two batches, a week apart, from the same sender to the same recipient, with the same four amounts and formats. There is no fan-out or return path. T2251 and T2252 bring in only AUD 3,995.12 before the second AUD 95,462.82 batch; the eight reported pass-through pairs are every combination of those two receipts and four payments, not evidence that the receipts funded the payments. The rows support an ordinary verdict but cannot prove the payments' legitimate purpose or reveal the IBM labels.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most false-ring runs treated exact weekly repetition and mixed payment formats as proof of structuring, despite the traffic staying on one account pair. Some also promoted time-adjacent, amount-mismatched receipts into a chain; the supplied pass-through count made that weak link look like eight corroborating paths.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Repeated batches between the same two accounts, even across payment formats, do not by themselves establish a scheme; do not call a chain merely because earlier receipts precede payments unless the amounts or other evidence credibly link the funds."
answer.system_fix: Add one computed fact beside pass-through pairs: T2251 and T2252 total AUD 3,995.12, versus AUD 95,462.82 in T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389 (4.2%); the eight pairs are generated from two receipts crossed with four payments.
answer.risk_of_fix: A real scheme could use recurring payments on one corridor or commingle small illicit receipts with larger balances. The rule must reject repetition as sufficient evidence, not categorically exempt such transfers.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The rows contain no structural marker of a scheme: 0 directed loops, all large flows are a single sender→single recipient corridor (80A3DE9A0→80A4A6D80, 8 transfers to exactly 1 distinct account, T0785/T0790/T0794/T0796 and the exact replay T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389 one week later), and the 'pass-through' pairs are spurious: only 635.64 (T2251) and 3359.48 (T2252) arrived at the hub against ~95,463 going out, so no funds were actually passed along. The exact four amounts repeated exactly 7 days apart across the same four formats is a signature of a scheduled batch payment run (payroll/settlement), not structuring — structuring splits one sum to evade a threshold, it does not replay identical cent-exact amounts weekly to the same counterparty.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models treated repetition plus format-mixing as intrinsically suspicious ('textbook structuring'), without checking that a real scheme needs either multiple counterparties, a return path, or matched funds moving on — none of which exist here. The code-provided 'pass-through pairs' fact actively hurt: pairing T2251/T2252 (total ~4k) with the 34k outflows nudged several models (haiku v2, deepseek v2, mistral v2, kimi v2) into inventing a chain they admitted didn't amount-match. Models that stayed ordinary (sonnet v5, grok v1, glm v1/v2, luna, sol v3-v5) succeeded precisely by reasoning 'one counterparty, no loop, inflows don't fund outflows, exact weekly repeat = scheduled payments'.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'Repetition is not suspicion. An identical set of amounts replayed between the same two accounts at a regular interval (e.g., exactly 7 days apart) is a scheduled payment run unless it also shows fan-out, fan-in, a cycle, or amount-matched forwarding. Before naming a chain or pass-through, check that incoming amounts roughly cover outgoing ones; a hub that received a few thousand and sent tens of thousands is not passing money through.'
answer.system_fix: Change the pass-through-pair code fact to only emit pairs where the outgoing amount is within, say, 70–130% of the incoming amount (drop all 8 pairs here, which pair 635.64/3359.48 with 12k–34k outflows), and add a new computed fact 'exact_replay: set of transfers with identical amounts and formats between the same account pair repeated N days apart' so models classify T0785-T0796 vs T2382-T2389 as a replay rather than rediscovering it as structure.
answer.risk_of_fix: Amount-matching the pass-through fact could hide genuine layering where a hub injects its own funds on top of a small passed-through amount, and the replay fact could excuse a real smurfing script that happens to replay a fixed set; mitigated by keeping the raw burst facts visible so a replay combined with fan-out or a cycle still flags.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only marker of T1154 is its size. At 295,050.93 MXN it is about 90x the neighborhood median (3,263.69), over 4x the next-largest transfer (T2623, 69,142.21), and about 97% of everything 80A440100 received. It is also an ACH, and every labeled laundering transfer in this slice is ACH. There is no structure to point to: no loop, no burst, and T2476 (1,054.91 USD into 80685EE50) comes six days after T1154, so it cannot be its source. The one pass-through pair the code found (T2303 -> T2623) involves the unlabeled T2303 and T2623, so following it leads to the wrong rows. Format and currency do not separate the label either, because 4 of 6 rows are ACH and 5 of 6 are MXN. The data therefore supports 'T1154 is the odd one out', but it cannot show that T1154 is laundering and not a large legitimate payment.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The prompt and facts pointed the models at multi-transfer shapes. Most of them looked for a shape, found a hub with mismatched amounts and a recurring-looking cheque pair (T0832/T2303), and answered ordinary. They treated T1154 as an 'isolated inbound with no onward movement' when its isolation and size are the only signal in the neighborhood. The runs that said ring (haiku v1, deepseek, kimi v1, glm, sonnet v2x) did include T1154. But they labeled a fan-in and added 3-4 innocent rows (T0150, T0832, T2303, sometimes T2623), which is the wrong unit of analysis for a lone ring.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "A 'lone' scheme has no structure by definition. If no loop, burst, chain or fan shape exists, still check whether a single ACH transfer is a clear outlier, for example more than 10x the neighborhood median and the largest transfer into its receiver. If so, answer pattern 'lone' and list only that one id. Do not add the receiver's other inflows, and do not let mismatched amounts at the hub count against a transfer that is flagged on size alone."
answer.system_fix: Add transfer-level facts, computed with file-wide baselines and not only within the six rows: each transfer's amount as a ratio to the neighborhood median and as a percentile of all ACH transfers in the same currency (ideally USD-equivalent), the transfer's share of its receiver's total inflow, and whether it is the receiver's largest inflow. Then add a second pass that scores single transfers on these facts and returns at most one id as a 'lone' candidate. Do not feed that pass the hub-level fan-in story.
answer.risk_of_fix: Large legitimate ACH payments (payroll, B2B settlements, property) would be flagged as lone rings. This neighborhood also has another large ACH, T2623, which is unlabeled, so a looser size threshold would flag it too. The fix needs a high file-wide percentile cutoff and a limit of one id per neighborhood, and even then precision will be modest because size alone is a weak tell.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1154 is a 295,050.93 MXN ACH into 80A440100, over 61 times that account’s next-largest visible incoming transfer (T0150, 4,821.18 MXN). That makes it a distinct lone-transfer review candidate, not proof of laundering. The only later outflow, T2623, is much smaller and occurs over six days later; T2476 reaches T1154’s sender after T1154, so it cannot fund it. Nothing in these rows establishes why IBM labeled T1154 illicit.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models looked for a multi-transfer scheme and treated the absence of a convincing chain, burst, or cycle as reason to call every row ordinary, missing the possibility of a lone labeled transfer. Models that called the neighborhood a fan-in did include T1154, but also accused ordinary inbound and outbound rows without evidence tying them to it.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Before deciding the neighborhood is ordinary, check whether one transfer is an extreme outlier against comparable payments into the same recipient; if so, consider it separately as a low-confidence lone candidate, and do not include neighboring transfers solely because they touch the same account.'
answer.system_fix: Add a per-recipient, same-currency incoming-amount comparison and a second-pass review trigger—not an automatic laundering verdict—when an ACH exceeds 50 times the next-largest comparable incoming transfer and at least three comparison transfers are visible. T1154 meets that trigger.
answer.risk_of_fix: A legitimate unusually large ACH could trigger review; treating the trigger as a laundering verdict would create false alarms.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: No labeled-scheme shape is in the rows. The only heavy corridor is one pair: 80A3DE9A0 to 80A4A6D80, the same four amounts and formats (34180.84 Cheque, 28735.64 Credit Card, 19908.12 ACH, 12638.22 Cash) as T0785, T0790, T0794, T0796 on 09/02 and again as T2382, T2384, T2387, T2389 on 09/09. Both bursts touch 1 counterparty, so they are not fan-out; there is no fan-in, no gather step, and 0 directed loops. The eight code pass-through pairs are unmatched: T2251 (635.64) and T2252 (3359.48) are about 4% of the ~95463 burst and cannot fund T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389. T0886, T1775, and T2518 are a separate small corridor with no return path. Week-apart exact replay to one counterparty is a scheduled payment, not layering.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most false rings (sonnet v1–v4, deepseek, mistral, kimi, sol v2, grok v2) read that exact weekly replay, especially the four-format split, as structuring, scatter-gather, or 'other', even though funds never leave a single ordered pair and never reassemble. v2 facts then added a second error: haiku v2, deepseek v2, mistral v2, and kimi v2 treated the unmatched 9-hour pass-through pairs as a chain, which is what flipped haiku from a correct ordinary call on raw rows.
answer.prompt_fix: Add this rule: Treat an exact replay of the same amounts from one account to the same single counterparty, days apart, as a scheduled payment, not a scheme; fan-out, fan-in, and scatter-gather require three or more distinct counterparties, and a chain requires a later outbound to be nearly the whole amount of a prior inbound, not a small credit paired with a much larger later debit.
answer.system_fix: Stop emitting pass-through pairs unless the later outbound is within 20% of that inbound (or a burst's outflows sum to roughly the inflows); tag single-counterparty bursts as scheduled-replay candidates rather than as pattern evidence. That unmatched pass-through list is what turned a correct v1 call into a ring.
answer.risk_of_fix: A real one-to-one structuring corridor with no third counterparty, or a chain that forwards only a fraction of each inbound (fees or partial splits), would be forced to ordinary. Labeled main-slice schemes are structural and ACH, so that miss is unlikely here, but the rule would hide genuine pair-only smurfing if it appears.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The eight suspicious rows are one sender-recipient pair, 80A3DE9A0 to 80A4A6D80: T0785, T0790, T0794, T0796 on 2022-09-02 and T2382, T2384, T2387, T2389 on 2022-09-09 repeat the same four amount/format pairs (34180.84 Cheque, 28735.64 Credit Card, 19908.12 ACH, 12638.22 Cash). Computed facts show 0 directed loops and no fan-out/fan-in: 80A3DE9A0 sent to 1 distinct account, and 80A4A6D80 received from 1 distinct account. The apparent pass-through from T2251 (635.64 ACH) and T2252 (3359.48 ACH) into 80A3DE9A0 before the second burst is an artifact of the 48-hour window: those inflows total 3,995.12 against 95,462.82 in T2382/T2384/T2387/T2389, about 4%, so no amount-matched forwarding is visible. T0886 and T1775 are an independent recurring 3,294.18 cheque between 80A3DECB0 and 80A879840, not connected to the main pair.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most ring reviewers over-weighted exact amount/format repetition and mixed payment formats between one counterparty pair, treating a weekly recurring batch as structuring or scatter-gather even though the facts showed one recipient, no return path, and no fan-out. Some v2 models also let the computed 48-hour pass-through pairs override the amount mismatch, calling T2251/T2252 the source of the second burst despite funding less than 5% of it. Models that followed the prompt's ordinary-traffic prior and required a cycle, fan shape, or amount-matched chain correctly returned ordinary.
answer.prompt_fix: Add this sentence after the existing sentence that says most neighborhoods are ordinary traffic: Exact repetition of a payment batch between the same two accounts, with the same amounts and payment formats (e.g. weekly), is recurring/scheduled business traffic, not laundering; do not call it structuring or scatter-gather unless there is also a cycle, fan-out/fan-in across multiple accounts, or an amount-matched pass-through. Do not infer a chain from a 48-hour pass-through pair alone unless the incoming amount is close to the outgoing amount.
answer.system_fix: none
answer.risk_of_fix: It could cause a model to skip real layering that uses identical repeated batches between one counterparty with no local cycle or amount-matched inflow, especially if the wider scheme is outside the neighborhood slice.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing structural marks T1154: 0 loops, 0 bursts, 1 pass-through pair that does not involve it, and it is just one of four inbound transfers to hub 80A440100. The only thing distinguishing it is magnitude: at 295,050.93 MXN it is ~90x the neighborhood median (3,263.69) and ~97% of all value in the slice, and per the bench's own known limits every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH and a 'lone' ring is a single labeled transfer. So the truth is recoverable only as 'the single large outlier ACH', not from any graph shape — the other five rows (including the tempting fan-in into 80A440100 and the T2303->T2623 pass-through) are unlabeled noise.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models split into two failure modes on the same trap: the fan-in shape around 80A440100. v1/raw-row models (and a few v2s) over-called the hub-and-spoke as a ring and flagged 3-5 ids, catching T1154 only incidentally. The v2-v5 models, correctly applying 'no loops, no bursts, mismatched pass-through amounts', talked themselves down to ordinary and flagged nothing — but they never applied the prompt's own stated heuristics (labeled = ACH, lone = one transfer) to ask 'if not a structure, is there one outlier transfer?'. Both camps treated 'lone' as a label for other cases, not as a live hypothesis for a neighborhood with a single dominant-value transfer.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'Before concluding ordinary, run a lone-transfer check: if the neighborhood has no ring structure but one transfer carries the large majority of the value (e.g. >80% of total and >20x the median) and is ACH, name pattern lone and flag that single transfer id. Do not flag its neighbors — a lone ring is exactly one transfer.'
answer.system_fix: Add one code fact: 'Largest single transfer: T1154 = 295,050.93 MXN, which is 97% of neighborhood value and 90x the median; flagged as lone-outlier candidate.' This makes the outlier explicit instead of requiring each model to compute ratios from raw rows, and pairs naturally with the existing known-limit that main-slice laundering is ACH.
answer.risk_of_fix: Legitimate large payments (payroll, rent settlement, one-off vendor payments into a busy collection account like 80A440100) will start getting flagged as 'lone', raising false alarms on exactly the busy-hub neighborhoods the prompt currently protects. The >80%-of-value plus >20x-median thresholds, and flagging only the single outlier id, keep the blast radius small, but on ordinary slices containing one big transfer this fix converts clean 'ordinary' verdicts into accusations against real customers.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: IBM labels only T1154 (80685EE50→80A440100, 295050.93 MXN ACH on 2022/09/03). The other five rows are not labeled: small ACH T0150 (4821.18), identical recurring cheques T0832 and T2303 (1706.19, one week apart, same sender), later USD credit T2476 (1054.91, after T1154 so it cannot fund it), and partial outflow T2623 (69142.21, ~23% of inflows, 6 days after T1154). Code facts show 0 loops, 0 bursts, and one amount-mismatched pass-through (T2303→T2623, 1706.19 then 69142.21). ACH is not distinctive (also T0150, T2476, T2623). Size marks T1154 as an outlier, not as laundering.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The labeled ring is lone: one transfer with no conserved multi-hop structure, so v2–v5 models that required loops, bursts, or amount-matched pass-through correctly refused a scheme and missed T1154. Runs that called ring misread hub 80A440100 (4 in from 3 senders) as fan-in or a cycle and attached unlabeled ids (T0150, T0832, T2303, T2623, sometimes T2476) even though the outflow does not match the collected sum.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Do not call fan-in because one account receives from several others. Fan-in needs several distinct senders and a later outflow that moves a substantial share of the collected amount within 48 hours. A single large transfer with no cycle, burst, or amount-conserving chain is not enough to call lone or any other scheme; return ordinary and flag no ids.'
answer.system_fix: Stop scoring lone labels (one labeled row, no conserved multi-hop) on this neighborhood prompt. Keep the prompt for multi-transfer patterns only; if lone detection is required, use a separate supervised single-transfer model trained outside this slice. Do not add an amount or ACH threshold to the facts fed here.
answer.risk_of_fix: The prompt change stops false fan-in alarms on busy hubs but still misses T1154-class labels. A separate lone model that thresholds on large ACH will false-alarm on ordinary large payments and on other ACH rows such as T0150, T2476, and T2623.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing in the structure marks T1766. It is a lone label, and the 804279E70/804279CE0 loop (T0486, T1768) that the code facts surface contains no labeled row. Weak per-transfer signals do point at it. T1766 (804279BF0 -> 804279E70, 2124.34, ACH) is the largest amount in the neighborhood. The next largest outflow from hub 804279BF0 is 681.89 (T0499), so T1766 is about 3x the hub's usual size. It is the hub's only ACH outflow; its other 13 sends are Cheque, Credit Card or Wire. It also goes to 804279E70, a counterparty the hub never paid before, while the hub's recurring payees are 808C21B70, 8082E7E90 and 80B7E0D00. Within 19 minutes, T1768 (1756.53 ACH, 804279CE0 -> 804279E70) arrives at the same account. The truth cannot be fully recovered, because T1768 looks just as suspicious and is unlabeled. So are T0486 and T1974, the other ACH rows. The data cannot say which ACH row IBM labeled.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models read 804279BF0 as a bill-paying hub, which is right for the repeated 130.96 and 396.78 payments, and then treated the whole neighborhood as ordinary. The only structure the code facts surfaced was the E70/CE0 loop, so the two models that flagged anything (Sonnet v1 and v5) chose T0486 and T1768 and missed T1766, the labeled transfer. They never compared T1766 with the hub's own history, where its format, size and new payee stand out, and the 'ordinary' answer lets an outlier through along with the recurring traffic. GPT-6 and Sonnet v2/v4 correctly saw the loop as weak evidence but then offered no fallback for a single suspicious transfer.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "A 'lone' ring is one transfer with no structure around it. If you see no pattern, do not stop at 'ordinary' and do not flag a loop or a repeated-amount series. Instead check each ACH transfer against its sender's own history, and name a lone ring only if exactly one transfer is both the largest of its sender's sends by at least 3x and goes to a counterparty that sender has never paid before. List only that id."
answer.system_fix: Add per-transfer code facts: for each transfer, the sender's median and max outgoing amount, the ratio of this amount to that median, whether the recipient is new for this sender, and whether the format differs from the sender's usual format. Provide a ranked 'outliers against sender history' list. For T1766 this would give about 3.1x the max of 681.89, a new payee, and a format unique to the hub's sends.
answer.risk_of_fix: It will flag unlabeled lookalikes: T1768 (large ACH to E70, 19 minutes later), T0486 (ACH), and T1974 (ACH into the hub), plus any ordinary large first-time payment in other neighborhoods. In this case it picks T1766 only because the single-id rule and the 3x-of-max test favor it, which is a thin margin. Precision on 'lone' will be low, and the ACH hint only works because this synthetic set labels ACH only, so it would not transfer to real data.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1766 is the only payment from 804279BF0 to 804279E70 and, at $2,124.34, is the largest transfer in this neighborhood. It is an ACH outflow that differs from BF0's repeated, smaller payments to other recipients. Those facts make it a review candidate, not proof of laundering: the rows do not show what the payment was for or any subsequent movement of its funds. The label on T1766 cannot be established from these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated the recurring payments as evidence that BF0's activity was ordinary and looked chiefly for a multi-transfer structure, missing the possibility of a single anomalous transfer. The runs that flagged the apparent E70–CE0 loop chose T0486 and T1768 instead; that path does not identify T1766 as laundering.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Before deciding ordinary, review each isolated ACH transfer that is unusually large for its sender and goes to a recipient that sender has not otherwise paid; report such a transfer as a candidate only when those independent anomalies are present, and do not claim its laundering label is proven by the rows."

answer.risk_of_fix: Legitimate one-off ACH payments, such as a large invoice, could meet the same criteria; treating the check as a conclusive label would create false alarms.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1154 is the only ACH transfer among the inbound legs and is an extreme amount outlier: 295,050.93 MXN vs median 3,263.69 (about 90x) and next largest 69,142.21. The other inbound transfers are small or recurring: T0150 4,821.18; T0832/T2303 identical 1,706.19 cheques. The bench's known ACH-only labeling rule makes T1154 the only eligible transfer. However, the six rows alone cannot prove T1154 is laundering rather than a legitimate large payment.

They treated 80A440100 as an ordinary busy hub and dismissed T1154 because its large amount did not reappear as a matching outflow and there were no bursts or loops. The v2 facts (0 loops, 0 bursts, one mismatched pass-through) reinforced the ordinary verdict, so no model applied the lone pattern to the extreme outlier.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1766 stands out as the only labeled laundering transfer and as the largest amount in the neighborhood: 2,124.34 USD vs median 291.48, sent by ACH from 804279BF0 to 804279E70, an account not in 804279BF0's usual recurring-payment pattern. Within 19 minutes the same recipient receives another large ACH, T1768 (1,756.53 from 804279CE0 to 804279E70). This pair looks like a one-off large funding event or gather, not the repeated cheque/credit-card flows from BF0. The v1 model instead flagged the T0486/T1768 loop, missing the actual labeled lone transfer T1766.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated 804279BF0's repeated identical payments as ordinary supplier/bill traffic and therefore discounted its one anomalous large ACH, T1766. They focused on explicit loops and fan-out/fan-in structures, so a single labeled transfer was invisible under the scheme definitions. None of the six runs flagged T1766 because it did not fit a full fan-out, fan-in, or cycle pattern and the prompt warned that busy accounts alone are not suspicious.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the scheme definitions: 'A lone scheme can be a single transfer. Flag a single ACH when it is an outlier for that sender, especially if it is the largest amount by far with no repeated counterpart, and even more so if the same recipient receives another large ACH within a short window; do not require a full fan-out, fan-in, or cycle.'
answer.system_fix: Compute two extra facts for each neighborhood before the model reads it: each transfer's amount as a multiple of the sender's median outbound amount, and the minutes until the next incoming transfer at the same recipient. Surface any ACH that is both >3x the sender's median outbound and has another incoming ACH at the same recipient within 60 minutes, which would surface T1766.
answer.risk_of_fix: The fix would create false alarms on legitimate large one-off ACH payments such as payroll, vendor invoices, or treasury sweeps that also arrive near other credits, especially in small neighborhoods where the sender's median is low.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing structurally unique marks T1766: it is a single ACH of 2,124.34 from hub 804279BF0 into 804279E70, and IBM's label attaches to it alone while the structurally more interesting rows (the T0486/T1768 two-hop loop, the repeated 130.96/396.78/291.48 payments) are all unlabeled. What does single it out, using only facts in the prompt, is the bench's own stated heuristics: 'every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH' and 'a lone ring is a single labeled transfer'. T1766 is the largest ACH in the window, lands in 804279E70 minutes before that account receives T1768 (1,756.53 ACH from 804279CE0), and E70 is one of only two ACH-heavy pass-through accounts. So the truth is recoverable only by combining the two-hop ACH cluster around E70 (T0486, T1766, T1768) with the ACH-only prior, not from the raw structure alone.
