The v1 runs and v5 noticed the loop but flagged T0486/T1768, the wrong rows. None of the runs applied the prompt's explicit known limits ('every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH', 'a lone ring is a single labeled transfer'), which were given precisely to crack cases like this.
answer.prompt_fix: Add a tie-breaker rule: 'If the neighborhood contains no scheme that fits the structural patterns, apply the known limits as a fallback: in this slice labeled laundering is ACH-only and a lone ring is one transfer, so name the single most anomalous ACH (largest, or feeding an account that also receives a same-format inflow shortly after, e.g. T1766 into 804279E70 ahead of T1768) as a low-confidence lone rather than answering ordinary.'
answer.system_fix: Add one computed fact: 'ACH-only transfers ranked by amount, and ACH transfers whose recipient receives another ACH within N hours', so the model sees T1766 -> E70 -> T1768 (19 min apart) as a highlighted pair instead of having to reconstruct it from raw rows; optionally run a second pass that, when verdict is ordinary, asks the model to pick the single most suspicious ACH under the stated priors.
answer.risk_of_fix: The fallback converts every truly-ordinary neighborhood into a forced low-confidence accusation against its largest ACH, creating false positives against customers making one big legitimate transfer, and it leans on a dataset artifact (ACH-only labels) that will not hold outside this slice.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Only T1126 is labeled (811334860 -> 8113348B0, 9884.18 Shekel, ACH, 2022/09/03 10:14). The other 16 rows are unlabeled: 14 fixed recurring payments from 810C151B0 (cash 1935.12 on T0501, T0749, T1129, T1219, T2038, T2200, T2320, T2683; cheque 1346.02 on T0744, T1130, T1218, T1532, T2323, T2681) and two large one-offs from 800948490 (T0767 ACH 147088.38, T0768 cheque 410132.05). 8113348B0 is a pure sink (received 17, sent 0); loops 0; pass-through 0; the only burst (T0744, T0749, T0767, T0768, 2 senders) does not include T1126. T1126 is not separable from T0767: both are cross-bank ACH one-offs into the same sink, and T0767 is larger. ACH is not a discriminator. The lone label is the simulator's mark, not a pattern in these rows.
answer.why_the_models_failed: No run named lone or flagged only T1126. Fan-in callers (haiku v1/v2, deepseek v1/v2, kimi v1/v2, glm v1/v2, grok v2, mistral v2, luna v1) treated every inflow to 8113348B0 as one scheme and flagged all 17 ids, burying the labeled row in 16 ordinary payments. Ordinary callers (sonnet v1-v5, sol v2-v5, luna v2, grok v1, mistral v1) correctly rejected that fan-in — three senders, a dominant fixed-amount series, no onward flow — then flagged nothing. sol v1 flagged the 14 recurring ids and missed T1126. The rows do not show which single transfer is the injection.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Fan-in requires many distinct senders, not one recurring fixed-amount payer plus one or two other inflows to a sink that never sends; do not flag that recurring series. Lone means exactly one transfer id, and only if these rows show a concrete anomaly that separates it from every other inflow. If you cannot separate it, answer ordinary and flag nothing — do not guess a lone id, and do not use payment format or a shared beneficiary as the anomaly.'
answer.system_fix: None inside this neighborhood. Do not add an ACH filter, a just-under-10000 rule, or a singleton-sender fact: ACH also selects unlabeled T0767, and a one-time payer into a busy beneficiary is ordinary. Exclude lone-labeled slices from the structural score, or join the simulator pattern id in a second pass the model never sees.
answer.risk_of_fix: The prompt rule stops false fan-in alarms on collector-plus-recurring neighborhoods, but it will still miss T1126 and every other lone injection that is not separable in the slice. Forcing a lone flag on the singleton sender would newly accuse ordinary one-off payments to shared beneficiaries.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The strongest shared structure is seven labeled inflows to 806698470 (T1920, T2171, T2386, T2403, T2430, T2435, T2439), followed by outflows T2441 and T2448. T2430 connects that hub to 804DE3CB0, which also participates in the apparent four-account loop through T0832, T1052, T0972 and T1036. This supports investigating one connected scatter-gather neighborhood, but not recovering all 13 labels exactly: the loop is not a time-ordered circulation, and same-endpoint, same-time parallel transfers T1038 and T1053 are unlabeled. The rows cannot prove which incoming funds financed either hub outflow.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The Claude runs concentrated on the conspicuous loop and missed its connection through T2430 to the later gathering hub; the v4 confidence rule then suppressed even that partial finding. GPT v2 found the seven-inflow hub and T2441 but stopped before the second outflow, T2448, and did not trace the connection back to the loop. Exact label membership is not fully inferable from transfer structure alone.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "When you find a cycle or a many-sender hub, check whether an account links them, and inspect all later outflows from that hub before choosing one pattern; do not include parallel transfers merely because they share endpoints, format, or timestamp."
answer.system_fix: Add a compact, time-ordered hub-neighborhood fact: list every inflow and outflow of accounts receiving from many distinct senders, plus one-hop links from those senders to any detected loop. Here it should expose T2430 as the loop-to-hub link and show both T2441 and T2448 as later hub outflows.
answer.risk_of_fix: A legitimate busy hub connected to an incidental graph loop could be overcalled. The added fact should prompt inspection, not automatically label every inflow, outflow, or parallel loop leg.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled ring has two visible parts joined at 804DE3CB0 and the hub 806698470. (1) The loop core: T0972, T1036, T0832, T1052 (7052.99 in T0832 and again in T1052). (2) The gather and exit around hub 806698470. Seven distinct senders each send one large, non-repeating ACH transfer: T1920 (803C16F80), T2171 (80422D430), T2386 (80CE8C910), T2403 (80107B480), T2430 (804DE3CB0), T2435 (80FDB9D80), T2439 (803498EF0). The hub then forwards in T2441 (68,984 Yuan to 807E2E610, 9 minutes after T2439) and T2448 (9,701.95 Euro to 80FDA64B0). T2430 comes out of the loop account 804DE3CB0, which ties the loop to the hub, so the whole thing is one scatter-gather. Hints that separate it from the surrounding noise: every labeled row is ACH, none of the labeled amounts recurs, and every row after 2022/09/10 13:10 except T2414 is labeled. Not recoverable: T1038 and T1053 (small parallel ACH rows inside the loop) and T2435 (475.74) look just like the unlabeled recurring ACH noise (T0435, T1029, T2025). T1038 and T1053 are unlabeled and T2435 is labeled, so no row-level feature separates them with certainty.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models saw the loop and the hub as two separate stories. Most flagged only the 4-row loop, and one (sonnet v1) explicitly dismissed the 806698470 inflow as 'a busy account', ignoring that the 8 distinct inbound senders were mostly one-off large ACH transfers and that T2430 links the loop to the hub. gpt-6-sol v2 found the hub (8 of 8 flagged rows labeled) but called it a fan-in and left out the loop and T2448. The v4 confidence rule then converted sonnet's correct-but-low-confidence ring call into 'ordinary', so the ring was missed entirely. Nobody produced the union of 13 rows, and the unlabeled decoys (recurring 803029B00 and 80102B720 flows, the big cash and cheque rows T1137 and T1144) added noise.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A ring may combine shapes. If a loop or chain account also sends to a hub that collects large one-off transfers from many different senders and forwards them within hours, report the loop, the gather and the exits as ONE scatter-gather and list all of those transfers. A hub with many distinct senders of non-repeating large ACH amounts is not just a busy account. Ignore identical amounts that recur on a schedule (for example the same sender-receiver pair repeating one amount).' Also remove the low-confidence downgrade to ordinary for cases where the model names specific transfer ids.
answer.system_fix: Add code facts at two levels. First, tag each transfer as recurring (the same sender, receiver and amount seen 2 or more times) or one-off, and report per account the number of distinct senders of one-off ACH transfers, plus whether any one-off ACH sender is itself inside a detected loop. Second, change the unit of analysis from the loop to the connected component of one-off ACH transfers, so the loop, the 806698470 gather and the exits are scored as one candidate. Replace the blanket 'low confidence becomes ordinary' rule with a second pass that re-asks on that component instead of discarding it.
answer.risk_of_fix: Over-merging: hub accounts with many unrelated one-off ACH inflows (payroll, merchants) would be flagged whole. It would also pull in unlabeled one-off ACH noise like T1607, and the small parallel loop rows T1038 and T1053 would be wrongly included. The ACH/one-off filter is a bench artefact and may not transfer to real data. Removing the downgrade lets more low-confidence guesses through as accusations.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Only T1766 is labeled, and it has no multi-hop structure: it is not in the sole directed loop (T0486 773.40 ACH 804279E70->804279CE0 on 09/01, returned by T1768 1756.53 ACH six days later; amounts do not match and neither is labeled). T1766 (09/07 22:36, 804279BF0->804279E70, 2124.34 ACH) is the neighborhood max and the only outbound from hub 804279BF0 that is ACH, to a payee BF0 never otherwise pays. BF0's other 13 sends are small recurring bills (130.96 cheque x4 to 808C21B70; 396.78 card x3 to 8082E7E90; plus small cheque/card/wire to 80B7E0D00). Other ACHs (T0486, T1768, T1974) are not pattern-breaks on a recurring sender, so the label is not uniquely forced by topology or by 'ACH=laundering'.
answer.why_the_models_failed: This is a lone ring: one labeled transfer with no fan, burst, matched pass-through, or cycle, so models that required those shapes called the neighborhood ordinary once they read BF0's repeated 130.96/396.78/291.48 as bills (claude v2/v4, both gpt runs). The only computed structure is the unmatched two-account loop, and claude v1/v5 flagged that distractor (T0486, T1768) instead of T1766. The prompt names 'lone' but never says a single format-and-payee break on an otherwise recurring account counts, so the miss is systematic.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: Lone rule — if there is no amount-matched cycle, fan, or chain, still return pattern lone and flag exactly one id when a sender whose other outflows are repeated identical amounts to a stable payee set has a single outbound that is (1) its only payment to that counterparty, (2) its only use of that payment format, and (3) several times its own median outbound (in this neighborhood that is only T1766); do not flag an unmatched two-account return such as T0486/T1768.
answer.system_fix: Emit a code fact lone_pattern_break listing transfer ids that meet those three tests, and a second pass that must consider that id as lone when the structural pattern is none; do not add an ACH-only or max-amount-only rule.
answer.risk_of_fix: A legitimate one-off (tax, insurance, new savings) that is large, in a format the account never otherwise sends, and to a brand-new payee on an otherwise recurring retail account would be flagged as a lone ring.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled chain is T1641 (80026F7B0 -> 800235EC0, 1294.26 EUR, ACH, 09/07 08:12) then T1862 (800235EC0 -> 80011AE70, 1509.99 USD, ACH, 09/08 10:00), about 26 h apart. Three things mark it. (1) It is the only ACH-in then ACH-out pair on the hub within 48 h. 800235EC0's other ACH sends (T0262, T0664, T0846, T0971, T1161) have no ACH feeder, and T1900, the only other later send, is a Wire. (2) The amounts are comparable, 1294 in and 1510 out, a change of about 17% with a currency switch. Every other hop the models examined moves a tiny fraction onward (1931.66 in, 17.28 out). (3) T1862 is the only transfer into 80011AE70, which then fans out 13 USD payments. Nothing proves laundering, though. The same hub has a near-identical feeder, T1639 (8001D8590, 3662.75, Cheque, 15 minutes before T1641) that is NOT labeled, and ACH alone is not discriminating (9 ACH rows, only 2 labeled). Nothing in the rows shows the rest of IBM's longer stack, so only the two-hop middle is visible.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every model called the neighborhood ordinary and flagged nothing. They explained away the two hubs as recurring customer activity. They also rejected pass-through because most in/out amounts differ greatly (e.g. 1931.66 in, 17.38 out), and so never separated the one hop with comparable amounts and a currency change. The listed pass-through facts pointed to T1639 -> T1862 (3662.75 to 1509.99), not T1641, so even a model inclined to flag would likely have picked the wrong feeder row.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A chain can be only two hops inside a busy hub. Do not dismiss a pass-through just because the hub's other traffic is recurring or small; test each incoming transfer against each outgoing transfer within 48 h and treat a pair as a chain candidate when the outgoing amount is within about 25% of the incoming one (a currency change does not break it). If exactly one such pair exists, flag both transfers and name the pattern chain.'
answer.system_fix: Replace the truncated pass-through list with a ranked one: for every in/out pair at an account within 48 h, give the amount ratio, whether the currency changed, and whether both payment formats match. List the ratio-near-1 pairs first. Optionally add a bench-only flag for ACH-in then ACH-out pairs, since the bench's labeled rows are all ACH. On this case that would isolate T1641 -> T1862 and rule out the Cheque feeder T1639. Run it as a second pass that only looks at the top 1-3 candidate pairs.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ratio-near-1 pairs are common on real payment hubs (payroll, rent, settlement), so this will raise false alarms outside synthetic data. The ACH-to-ACH filter exploits a quirk of this data set and would not transfer to real traffic. A 25% band might also have flagged T1639 -> T1862 (3662.75 to 1509.99 is off by more than 25%, so it would be excluded, but nearby cases may not be). Flagging a single pair in an otherwise ordinary neighborhood costs a customer review for what may be benign.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Two connected structures are fully visible in the rows/facts. (1) The cycle: 8042BFA00 -> 80E12A290 (T1036, 8012.60) -> 804DE3CB0 (T0832, 7052.99) -> 811F41AC0 (T1052, exact same 7052.99) -> back to 8042BFA00 (T0972, 6837.96); the computed loop facts list exactly this 4-account cycle with exact-amount preservation on two legs. (2) The gather: account 806698470 received from 8 distinct senders, and 7 of those inflows are the labeled fan-in legs T1920, T2171, T2386, T2403, T2430, T2435, T2439 (all ACH, all US Dollar, 475.74 to 14297.01, from otherwise-quiet accounts), followed by consolidation legs T2441 (68984.01 Yuan, 9 minutes after the last receipt) and T2448 (9701.95 Euro) out of 806698470. The 'all labeled transfers are ACH' and 'USD in, foreign-currency lump out' tells match the bench's known limits.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every run fixated on the small, salient 4-account cycle (exact amount 7052.99 repeated) and treated the fan-in into 806698470 as 'a busy account', which the prompt explicitly tells them not to flag on its own — so 9 of the 13 labeled transfers went unflagged. The one run that did read the gather correctly (gpt-6-sol v2, fan-in, 8/8 labeled) shows the evidence was sufficient; the failure was attention, not missing data. Separately, the v4 confidence rule converted a correct low-confidence ring call into 'ordinary / 0 ids', the worst possible outcome — a hedged but right answer was mechanically erased.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the pattern definitions: 'A busy account is not suspicious by itself, but if one account receives from many distinct senders that each send ONLY to it (in-degree high, senders' out-degree 1) and then moves a lump sum out shortly after the last receipt — especially in a different currency — that is a gather, not ordinary traffic; flag the inflows and the consolidation leg(s).' Also change the confidence rule to: 'if you see a concrete structure (named loop, named gather) with cited ids, report it at whatever confidence you have; never convert a structured finding into ordinary solely because confidence is low.'
answer.system_fix: Add one code fact: 'collector candidates' — accounts with in-degree >= 4 whose senders each have out-degree 1 in the neighborhood, plus whether a single large outbound transfer leaves within 24h of the last inflow and in a different currency. Here that would have surfaced 806698470 (8 senders, most sending only to it; T2441 9 minutes after T2439, USD->Yuan) as a named fact, forcing models to either flag or explicitly rebut it. Also replace the v4 downgrade-to-ordinary post-processing with downgrade-to-review (ring at low confidence keeps verdict ring, confidence low).
answer.risk_of_fix: The collector-candidate fact will fire on legitimate hubs (payroll, utility collection, exchange accounts) where many customers pay one merchant, and the 'senders' out-degree 1' guard may not hold in denser neighborhoods, producing fan-in false alarms. Removing the low-confidence downgrade will let some wrong low-confidence ring calls through as flagged, lowering precision on noisy slices.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1641 (80026F7B0 → 800235EC0, EUR 1,294.26, ACH) precedes T1862 (800235EC0 → 80011AE70, USD 1,509.99, ACH) by 25 hours 48 minutes. They form a two-transfer chain, and this is the only time-ordered ACH-to-ACH path through 800235EC0 in the rows. The rows do not establish that the money in T1641 funded T1862: T1639 also paid 800235EC0 shortly before T1862, and no balance or FX-conversion record is supplied. The exact IBM labels are therefore not provable from these transfers alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated a chain as requiring closely matched nominal amounts or a more conspicuous pass-through, then let the absence of loops and bursts support an ordinary verdict. That missed the short ACH-to-ACH path T1641 → T1862; comparing its EUR and USD amounts directly was particularly uninformative. Repeated payments elsewhere in the neighborhood made the two legs easier to dismiss as background traffic.
answer.prompt_fix: Before concluding ordinary, check time-ordered A→B→C paths within 48 hours in which both transfers are ACH; assess each as a possible short chain even without a loop, burst, or equal nominal amounts, but do not call it laundering on that structure alone.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact listing ACH-to-ACH two-transfer paths within 48 hours, including elapsed time, currencies, and other recent inflows to the middle account. Here it would surface T1641 → T1862 alongside the competing inflow T1639.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ordinary accounts can receive and send ACH payments within 48 hours. Automatically flagging every such path would create false alarms; the added check should surface candidates, not assign labels.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Two ACH structures are visible. (1) The cycle: 811F41AC0 -> 8042BFA00 (T0972, EUR 6837.96) -> 80E12A290 (T1036, USD 8012.6) -> 804DE3CB0 (T0832, USD 7052.99) -> 811F41AC0 (T1052, USD 7052.99); T0832 and T1052 have the exact same amount, and the path returns to the starting account. (2) The gather: seven distinct accounts send ACH into 806698470 (T1920, T2171, T2386, T2403, T2430, T2435, T2439), then 806698470 sends two large ACH legs out: T2441 (Yuan 68,984.01) and T2448 (Euro 9,701.95). Account 804DE3CB0 bridges the two structures: it receives T0832 in the cycle and later sends T2430 into 806698470. Individual sparse legs such as T2435 and the foreign-currency outbound T2448 are not independent proof from rows alone, but are recoverable as part of the linked cluster.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated the cycle and the fan-in as separate single-pattern findings and never merged them through the shared account 804DE3CB0. Claude v1/v2/v5 reported only the four-account cycle, and v4's confidence rule suppressed even that low-confidence true positive because the timestamps were not in perfect loop order. GPT v2 reported only the fan-in into 806698470, omitted the cycle and T2448, and used the USD/Yuan currency mismatch as a reason to hedge rather than treating it as one linked scatter-gather ring.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A laundering scheme may combine multiple patterns; if two suspicious groups share an account, report them together and list every transfer in the combined group, including outbound legs in a different currency, and do not downgrade a low-confidence cycle to ordinary merely because its timestamps are out of order.'
answer.system_fix: Add a shared-account ACH cluster fact: compute the connected component of ACH transfers that share an account with any detected pattern. Here that component would link the cycle and the 806698470 fan-in through 804DE3CB0, producing the full candidate set T0832,T0972,T1036,T1052,T1920,T2171,T2386,T2403,T2430,T2435,T2439,T2441,T2448 before the model makes its final verdict.
answer.risk_of_fix: A shared-account union can over-include legitimate ACH activity around busy nodes. In this neighborhood it could falsely pull in T2025 (804DE0920 -> 804DE3CB0) or T1607 because those accounts touch 804DE3CB0 or 803498EF0. The fix must require a suspicious ACH pattern plus shared-account linkage, not simply all ACH transfers in the connected component.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1641 and T1862 form the only ACH-in/ACH-out pair through the same account within 48h in this neighborhood: T1641 (80026F7B0 -> 800235EC0, 1,294.26 EUR ACH) arrives 2022-09-07 08:12, and T1862 (800235EC0 -> 80011AE70, 1,509.99 USD ACH) leaves 2022-09-08 10:00, a 25.8h chain through 800235EC0. The supplied pass-through facts hid this pair by requiring outgoing amount <= incoming amount, and instead showed T1639 -> T1862. 80026F7B0 had just moved a huge amount out via T0712, and 80011AE70 receives this ACH before continuing its outgoing fan.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v2+ models depended on the computed pass-through facts, which omitted the actual labeled chain because T1862's raw amount (1,509.99) exceeded T1641's raw amount (1,294.26), even though the currencies differ. The models then treated the hubs' repeated fixed-size payments as normal recurring activity and did not test the ACH-in/ACH-out chain signature that isolates T1641 and T1862 in this neighborhood.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'In this synthetic data every labeled laundering transfer is ACH; if an ACH arrives at an account and an ACH leaves that same account within 48 hours, flag both transfer ids as a chain candidate even if the outgoing amount is larger or in a different currency. Do not require amount conservation for a chain.'
answer.system_fix: In the computed facts, add ACH-in/ACH-out pass-through pairs within 48h without an outgoing-amount <= incoming-amount condition. For this neighborhood that fact should explicitly emit T1641 -> T1862 (25.8h, ACH EUR to ACH USD).
answer.risk_of_fix: Other legitimate ACH pass-throughs within 48h, such as merchant settlement, payroll, or treasury sweeps, could become false positives; this needs a second-pass filter using account roles, amounts, or frequency.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled transfer T2372 (80D9BF830 -> 80D9BFE70, 18306.45 Euro, Cheque, 2022/09/10 10:42) stands out only on size and timing. Its amount is about 2.1x the next largest (8713.48 on the recurring cheque) and about 6x the other 80D9BF830 -> 80D9BFE70 transfers (T0580 2728.32, T2336 3130.32). It is also the last row, and it follows 80D9BF830's inflows that had been small and recurring. Nothing structural marks it: it is not part of a distinct loop, burst or chain beyond the generic hub activity around 80D9BF830/80D9BFE70. It is also a Cheque, although the bench notes say labeled transfers in the main slice are ACH. That contradicts the label, so format is a misleading tell here, not a usable one. The label itself cannot be inferred from the rows with confidence. A big-amount outlier at the end of an active pair is only a weak hint.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The ring is a single labeled transfer with no structure, so the models either called the whole neighborhood ordinary (recurring identical payments like T0504/T0670/T1170 and the T0629/T2066 repeats look like business) or latched onto the 80D9BF830<->80D9BFE70 back-and-forth as a cycle and flagged 5 ids, of which only T2372 was labeled. The two runs that said ring (sonnet v5, gpt v2) found it by accident through the loop facts, with the wrong pattern and wrong ids, and they hedged that amounts do not match. No model isolated the single outlier transfer.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A lone ring is one transfer that breaks its own pair's or account's pattern, for example a one-off amount far above that pair's usual transfers. If the structure is otherwise recurring or ordinary, name that single transfer with pattern lone and list only its id; do not list the other pair transfers as a cycle just because they run in both directions.'
answer.system_fix: Add a per-pair amount-outlier fact computed by code: for each directed account pair, flag transfers above about 3x the pair's median amount, with the ratio and the rank among all rows (e.g. T2372 at 18306.45 vs the pair's others of 1489 to 3130). Also flag recurring identical-amount series (the 8713.48 cheque x7) so that models can discount them. Add a second pass that, when a cycle is suspected, asks which single transfer is the outlier.
answer.risk_of_fix: Outlier flags will fire on ordinary large one-off payments, such as business settlements or the first payment of a new series, and will raise false alarms on legitimate customers. Because lone rings are rare and look like any big payment, precision will be low. In this data a single big cheque at the end of a hub pair is also weakly labeled evidence, so the fix may yield one right flag among many wrong ones.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled rows form exactly the two-hop fragment the bench calls a chain: T1641 (80026F7B0 -> 800235EC0, 1294.26 EUR, ACH, 2022/09/07 08:12) is followed ~26 hours later by T1862 (800235EC0 -> 80011AE70, 1509.99 USD, ACH, 2022/09/08 10:00), an in-then-out through hub 800235EC0 with an amount ratio of 0.86 — far closer than any other pass-through pair in the facts (e.g. T0371 1931.66 in vs T0664 17.38 out). Both labeled rows are ACH, matching the prompt's own hint that every labeled laundering transfer in this slice is ACH. But the computed 'pass-through pairs' fact shown to the models lists 10 pairs including T1639->T1862 yet never pairs T1641 with T1862, and nothing else in the rows (0 loops, 0 bursts, no gather) distinguishes this chain from the heavy recurring-payment noise around it.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs anchored on the absence of loops and bursts and on the gross amount mismatches in the listed pass-through pairs, concluding 'no chain' because money in never visibly matched money out. They never tested the one pair where in and out amounts nearly match (T1641/T1862), partly because the code facts never surfaced that pairing, and they ignored the prompt's 'all labeled transfers are ACH' hint, which would have cut the candidate set from 35 rows to the 9 ACH rows containing both labels.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the scheme definitions: 'A chain is money passed through one intermediate within 48 hours where the outgoing amount is within roughly 30% of the incoming amount (fees or currency conversion may shift it); when judging pass-through pairs, compare amounts and payment format, and treat same-format (especially ACH) near-matching amounts as the tell, not exact equality.' Also change the closing instruction to: 'If any pass-through pair matches this profile, name it as a candidate chain with its transfer ids even at low confidence, rather than returning ordinary.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact that, for each pass-through pair, computes the out/in amount ratio and flags pairs with ratio between 0.5 and 2.0 and matching payment format; here T1641->T1862 (ratio 0.86, ACH/ACH) would rank first and T1639->T1862 (0.41) and the tiny-fraction pairs would rank below it. Also ensure the pair list is complete — T1641->T1862 is within the 48-hour window but absent from the 10 pairs the models were shown.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ranking pass-through pairs by amount similarity will occasionally promote innocent look-alikes — e.g. a refund or matched payroll in-and-out — and the prompt change pushes models to name a candidate chain instead of saying ordinary, which will convert some current true-negative neighborhoods into low-confidence false flags that a human must clear.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T2372 is the largest transfer (€18,306.45), a cheque on a pair whose other transfers are smaller ACH payments, and the last row shown. Those facts make it a transaction-level review candidate, but neither its amount, format nor timing establishes laundering or uniquely recovers IBM's label. The labeled scheme is lone: T2372 alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The ordinary verdicts let recurring payments elsewhere in the neighborhood obscure an unusual individual transfer. The ring verdicts noticed T2372 but treated reciprocal transfers as a labeled cycle, flagging four additional rows even though IBM labels only T2372; the computed loops establish account connectivity, not which transfers laundered money.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Assess each materially unusual transfer as a possible lone candidate even when surrounding traffic looks routine, but do not label it laundering—or add reciprocal transfers to its scheme—without transaction-specific corroboration.'
answer.system_fix: Route individual outliers such as T2372 to a separate review using account history or external investigative evidence; do not convert an amount, format or latest-timestamp rule into an automatic laundering verdict. If only these rows are available, the exact IBM label cannot be established.
answer.risk_of_fix: A review queue will include legitimate large cheques; automatically flagging them would create false alarms.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The label is only T1641 (80026F7B0->800235EC0, 1294.26 EUR ACH, 2022/09/07 08:12, banks 023->011) and T1862 (800235EC0->80011AE70, 1509.99 USD ACH, 2022/09/08 10:00, banks 011->010). answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Call a chain only if the hops you list roughly conserve amount in one currency or with an explicit FX; a two-hop path with mismatched amounts, a currency change, or many similar pass-throughs is not a scheme — return ordinary.' answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled transfer is T2372 (2022/09/10 10:42, 80D9BF830 -> 80D9BFE70, 18306.45, Cheque). Nothing in the structure marks it: the bench itself read the shape as 'lone', and T2372 sits inside a plausible two-account business exchange (T0412, T0580, T1470, T2336 are unlabeled counterparts of the same pair). What singles T2372 out is only circumstantial: it is by far the largest amount in the neighborhood (18306.45 vs median 4315.53), it is the last transfer in the window, and it is the only Cheque on the 830->E70 leg while every other transfer on that leg is ACH. Per the bench's own stated limits ('a lone ring is a single labeled transfer', 'rows after 2022-09-10 are mostly labeled'), a single large, format-breaking, window-closing transfer is the recoverable tell, but no code fact currently surfaces amount-outlier or format-change-on-a-pair, so the truth is not derivable from the facts the models were given.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The neighborhood is dominated by obvious recurring-payment noise (seven identical 8713.48 cheques from 80B695690, week-apart duplicates from 801EE3800/80D9BF8D0/80D9BFEC0), so most runs wrote the whole thing off as ordinary business and never scrutinised the single anomalous transfer. When v5 and gpt v2 did react, they latched onto the computed 2-account 'loops' and pass-through pairs between 80D9BF830 and 80D9BFE70 and flagged a 5-id cycle, which is structurally just two accounts trading both directions — a false-positive pattern the prompt's cycle definition invites. No run had a fact that isolates T2372 (largest amount, only non-ACH on that leg, last in window), so the lone ring was invisible either way.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A cycle needs 3 or more distinct accounts returning to the start; two accounts trading in both directions is not a cycle. If the neighborhood is mostly recurring identical payments but contains one transfer that breaks the pattern (much larger amount, different payment format on that account pair, or the last transfer in the window), consider verdict lone and flag only that transfer id.'
answer.system_fix: Add two code facts: (1) per account-pair, flag transfers whose payment format differs from the pair's dominant format or whose amount is more than ~3x the neighborhood median (this would surface T2372: only Cheque on 830->E70, 18306.45 vs median 4315.53); (2) restrict the directed-loops fact to loops through at least 3 distinct accounts so 2-account back-and-forth is no longer presented as a 'loop'.
answer.risk_of_fix: Amount/format outlier flags will fire on legitimate one-off large payments (e.g. a final invoice settling a series of small ones), and dropping 2-account loops could hide genuine two-party round-tripping schemes; net effect is likely a small rise in lone false positives in exchange for removing recurring 2-account cycle false positives.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Ground truth is a lone ring: only T2372 (80D9BF830→80D9BFE70, 18306.45 Euro Cheque, 2022/09/10 10:42) is labeled, 1 of 22 rows. It is the max amount and the only Cheque on a corridor whose other legs are smaller ACH (T0412 2550.93, T0580 2728.32, T1470 1489.08, T2336 3130.32), but size and format do not show placement or the same funds moving. answer.why_the_models_failed: Four runs (claude v1/v2/v4, gpt v1) correctly saw recurring identical amounts and unequal two-way trade and called the neighborhood ordinary, so they never emitted T2372. Two runs (claude v5, gpt v2) treated the computed 2-node loops as a cycle and flagged five ids, of which only T2372 is labeled, because the loop fact does not separate the labeled cheque from T0412, T0580, T1470 and T2336. answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A back-and-forth between only two accounts is not a cycle unless the same or nearly the same amount returns through 2 or more hops; unequal exchange (T0412, T0580, T1470, T2336, T2372) is ordinary. Do not flag a lone transfer just because it is the largest amount or sits on a loop. If no transfer is suspicious on its own, answer ordinary.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact that labels 2-node loops with non-matching amounts as exchange_not_cycle and drop them from the loop list the model sees. Do not add an amount-outlier or format rule aimed at T2372. No second pass on this neighborhood can recover the lone label.
answer.risk_of_fix: The prompt and loop-fact change stop false cycle flags on two-account trade but leave lone recall at zero, including T2372. A rule that instead flags the max amount or a Cheque on an ACH corridor would false-alarm on legitimate large or one-off payments, including scheduled cheques like the 8713.48 series.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair is T0959 (80832A480 -> 805D535A0, 673,831.65 Rupee, ACH) followed by T1211 (805D535A0 -> 802D21780, 7,548.74 Euro, ACH). Together they form the chain 80832A480 -> 805D535A0 -> 802D21780. Four things in the rows point at it. (1) 805D535A0 received 13 transfers but sent exactly one, T1211, so that is its only exit. (2) T1211 is a currency switch: the hub only ever receives Rupee, and this outflow is Euro, ACH, to a never-seen-before account. (3) T0959 is the largest amount in the set and appears once, while every other big payment repeats on a fixed pair (318,120.12 three times, 22,544.09 seven times). (4) Of the 4 ACH rows, T0862 and T2153 are an identical recurring pair (8,664.47), which leaves T0959 and T1211 as the only non-recurring ACH rows. The amounts also roughly agree once currency is normalized. 673,831.65 Rupee is on the order of 7.5k-8.5k Euro at any plausible rate, which fits T1211, and the Euro inflows into 80832A480 (T0860, T0862, T0912, about 9.8k total) are the same order of magnitude. The truth is not fully recoverable. The funds behind T0959 have no clean source in this window, and the rest of IBM's longer stack lies outside the neighborhood. The code's pass-through detector missed T1211 because the gap from T0959 is 48.3 h, just outside its 48 h window.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs compared raw numbers across currencies (673,831.65 Rupee vs about 9.8k Euro) and concluded the amounts 'don't match', so they rejected the 80832A480 pass-through. They never linked T0959 to T1211 because the code facts showed no pass-through at 805D535A0 (the 48 h window missed it by about 20 minutes). The large pool of recurring identical payments into the hub also pulled them toward 'ordinary recurring traffic', and none of them noticed that T0959 and T1211 are the only one-off ACH rows.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Never judge whether amounts match across different currencies by raw number. A Rupee amount about 80-90 times a Euro amount is a plausible conversion. Treat a large one-off transfer into a hub, followed by a single outflow in a different currency to a new account, as a chain candidate. Repeated identical payments on a fixed pair are recurring traffic. A non-repeating transfer of a different kind (different format or currency) inside that traffic is not.'
answer.system_fix: Add two code facts. (a) Currency-normalized amounts using a fixed rate table, with pass-through pairs shown as a ratio, e.g. 'T0959 673,831.65 INR is about 8.1k EUR vs T1211 7,548.74 EUR'. (b) Widen the pass-through window to 72 h, or list near-misses, so that T0959 -> T1211 (48.3 h) is reported. Optionally add a 'singleton' fact marking transfers whose (from, to, amount) never repeats, and one marking an account's only outbound transfer when it has many inbound ones.
answer.risk_of_fix: Currency-normalized matching and a longer window will create more candidate pass-throughs among ordinary busy accounts, especially hubs with many inbound and few outbound transfers, which are common in this data. The 'one-off ACH' hint leans on the slice quirk that labeled rows are all ACH, so it may not carry to other slices. A 72 h window is also tuned to this single case. Expect some new false flags on ordinary conversions and on recurring payroll-style hubs.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0959 (80832A480→805D535A0) and T1211 (805D535A0→802D21780) form a two-hop ACH chain. The second hop occurs 48 hours 19 minutes after the first, just outside the supplied 48-hour pass-through calculation, and is 805D535A0's only outgoing transfer. This makes the labeled pair a candidate the models should have examined, but the rows cannot establish that T1211 moved funds from T0959: the amounts and currencies differ substantially. ACH is not a unique label tell either; T0862 and T2153 are also ACH.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The computed pass-through list omitted T0959→T1211 by 19 minutes, and the models treated that omission, the amount mismatch, and the currency change as reasons to rule out onward movement. They consequently called the neighborhood ordinary without assessing the visible two-hop ACH chain as a candidate.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "For a possible chain, inspect successive transfers through the same account for at least 72 hours; do not treat exclusion from the 48-hour pass-through list, a currency change, or unequal amounts as proof that no chain exists, but distinguish a structural candidate from proven movement of the same funds."
answer.system_fix: Add a second-pass code fact listing ACH-to-ACH bridges within 72 hours, including elapsed time and whether the intermediary has other outgoing transfers. It would surface T0959→T1211 without automatically labeling it.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ordinary accounts can make successive ACH payments, including in different amounts and currencies. Automatically calling every such bridge laundering would create false alarms; no rule using these rows alone can guarantee the IBM labels are recovered without that risk.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled transfer is T2372, an 18,306.45 Cheque from 80D9BF830 to 80D9BFE70. It is the largest outflow from 80D9BF830 by far: the account's other outflows are T0580 (2,728.32) and T2336 (3,130.32). Before T2372, 80D9BF830 had received 12 payments from 5 distinct accounts, including the burst T0629/T0632/T0634 from 801EE3800 and recurring small payments T0655/T2241, T0682/T2165, plus T0412/T1470 from the eventual recipient 80D9BFE70. This looks like consolidation of prior inflows. But the same neighborhood also contains strong ordinary explanations: 80B695690 sends seven identical 8,713.48 cheques to 80D9BFE70 (T0504, T0670, T1170, T1397, T1717, T1924, T2022), and other senders repeat fixed amounts. So the row features narrow but do not uniquely identify T2372 absent IBM's label.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v1/v2/v4 runs demanded a clear multi-transfer pattern and, seeing unequal amounts in the back-and-forth between 80D9BF830 and 80D9BFE70 (T0412/T0580, T1470/T2336/T2372), dismissed it as ordinary recurring business and never tested the lone pattern. The v5 and GPT v2 runs relaxed the amount-match requirement and flagged a cycle, but the computed loops made them list all five back-and-forth legs, producing four false positives and still missing the true lone shape.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A lone scheme can be a single outbound transfer from a pass-through account that is an outlier in size and format relative to that account's other outflows; when you see such an outlier in the supplied facts, flag only that transfer under lone, not every back-and-forth leg.'
answer.system_fix: In the code facts, add a per-account outbound-outlier line: for 80D9BF830, the largest outbound is T2372 (18,306.45), 5.8x the next-largest T2336 (3,130.32) and the only Cheque outbound from that account.
answer.risk_of_fix: It will newly flag legitimate single large payments from cash-gathering accounts, such as a business paying a supplier, tax, or treasury consolidation, because account-level features without KYC cannot distinguish these from laundering.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0959 (80832A480 to 805D535A0, 673,831.65 Rupee, ACH) is the laundering inflow, and T1211 (805D535A0 to 802D21780, 7,548.74 Euro, ACH) is the onward leg 48h19m later; the amounts match after FX conversion at about 89.27 INR/EUR. 805D535A0 receives 13 transfers but makes only one outgoing transfer, T1211, and both labeled transfers are ACH, matching the bench rule. The repeated Rupee cheques into 805D535A0 are distractor ordinary traffic.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The code facts only listed same-currency pass-throughs within 48 hours, so T0959 to T1211 was not shown as a connected chain; the gap missed the 48h window by 19 minutes and the currencies differed. The models then treated the Rupee/Euro mismatch as evidence against onward movement and focused on the recurring identical-amount payments as ordinary traffic.
answer.prompt_fix: For chain detection, do not require the same currency: convert amounts to a common currency at plausible FX rates before deciding whether an outgoing transfer continues an incoming payment, and extend the look-forward window to 72 hours. Example: 673,831.65 Rupee in T0959 is about 7,548.74 Euro in T1211.
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact for FX-normalized pass-through pairs within 72 hours, specifically listing 80832A480 to 805D535A0 to 802D21780 via T0959 then T1211 with the converted amounts.
answer.risk_of_fix: It may flag legitimate cross-border trade, FX conversion, or remittance payments where a currency change and 2-3 day settlement are normal; false positives can be reduced by requiring both legs to be ACH and the intermediate account to have no other relationship to the destination.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled chain is A→B→C: 80832A480 --T0959 (673831.65 Rupee ACH)--> 805D535A0 --T1211 (7548.74 Euro ACH)--> 802D21780, two days later. The recoverable markers are: (1) both labeled transfers are ACH, and the bench's own hint says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH, yet only 4 of 22 rows here are ACH (T0862, T0959, T1211, T2153) — a 2-of-4 hit the models could have exploited; (2) T1211 is the ONLY transfer 805D535A0 ever sends despite receiving 13, i.e. a single outlier onward hop from a fan-in sink, which is exactly what turns a fan-in into a chain; (3) T0959 is a 30x outlier vs the median 22544.09. What is NOT recoverable: why T0959/T1211 are laundering while the identical-looking recurring Rupee payments are not, and the amounts/currencies genuinely do not match across hops, so a human would not call this laundering on these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models anchored on the dominant legitimate-looking traffic (repeated identical Rupee payments from 804BD4BF0 and 804FE11E0 into 805D535A0) and treated 805D535A0 as a busy recipient, so they never constructed the two-hop path T0959→T1211. When they did examine 80832A480, the pass-through framing hurt them: they compared small Euro inflows (T0860/T0862/T0912) against the big Rupee T0959, found the amounts and currencies mismatched, and dismissed the whole account as a dead end — never checking what 805D535A0 did next (T1211). The computed facts listed 0 loops and only same-direction pairwise pass-throughs, none of which pointed at the actual chain, so every prompt version had no fact that surfaced the chain shape.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the scheme guidance: 'A chain does not require matching amounts or currencies across hops — layering often converts value. If an account receives a large transfer and later makes even one onward transfer, treat that onward hop as part of the candidate chain and list both ids. Also: when only a small minority of rows share one payment format, and the labeled base rate for that format is high, weigh those rows heavily before dismissing the neighborhood.'
answer.system_fix: Change the pass-through fact: instead of only pairwise A→B→C within 48h, emit full reachable paths of length 2-3 through the neighborhood regardless of amount/currency match, and flag any account whose out-degree is exactly 1 against a large in-degree (here 805D535A0: 13 in, 1 out via T1211) as a 'sink-with-single-egress' — that fact alone points at the T0959→T1211 chain.
answer.risk_of_fix: Dropping the amount/currency-matching expectation will make models flag more benign chains (e.g. a customer who aggregates then pays one bill), raising false positives on fan-in-then-pay-out accounts; sink-with-single-egress also fires on ordinary savings or payroll-aggregator accounts, so it should rank candidates for review, not auto-accuse.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The hub is plainly visible. Account 100428930 sent 20 transfers to 18 distinct accounts, never received anything, and sits upstream of every pass-through pair the code found (T1262->T1363 via 80D61AF60, and T1579->T1727/T1809/T1810 via 80D5E56F0). All 9 labeled ids (T0233, T0600, T1003, T1025, T1262, T1458, T1480, T1484, T1579) leave that hub, so the fan-out reading is right. The exact membership is not recoverable, though. The hub has 11 other outgoing rows that are unlabeled (T0215, T0265, T0405, T0630, T0964, T1044, T1368, T1820, T1851, T2349, T2406). Amount, format, bank and timing do not separate the two groups. The labeled set mixes tiny amounts (T1484 10.85, T0233 118.71, T1458 181.75) with larger ones (T1579 41,534.65, T1480 9,816.43). None of the labeled rows is ACH, so the format tell from the bench notes does not apply on this slice. The only weak signal is that 7 of the 9 labeled recipients also appear elsewhere in the neighborhood (80D61AF60, 80D5E56F0, 80D6D4030, 80D5F5C50, 80D785770, 80CE17920, 80CF5B3C0). Most unlabeled recipients are leaf accounts with no other activity, such as 80D9CFB90, 80D92B060 and 80D5C0D10. T0630 (470,576.50) and T2406 (112,419.20) are the largest hub rows, yet they are unlabeled.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every model found the hub and then explained it away as a business paying many counterparties, citing the varied amounts, mixed formats and 10-day spread. They treated 'no inbound, no return, no burst' as evidence of innocence, when a fan-out source has none of those by definition. The recurring identical flows (80CFD00B0->80D5F5C5, 80D61AF60->80D815530, 80CF63F30->80D6D4030) pulled attention to noise. The pass-through pairs were dismissed because the amounts did not match (1,559.58 in, 256,045.73 out), which is correct for the amounts but misses that the hub rows are the labeled part. The prompt's 'busy accounts are not suspicious' and 'wrong accusation costs a customer' pushed them to a default verdict of ordinary.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'An account with many outgoing transfers (about 10 or more) to many distinct recipients (about 10 or more) and no inbound transfers is a fan-out candidate. Varied amounts, mixed formats and a spread over days do not rule it out, because fan-out sources look like that. If its recipients also show onward or other activity, answer fan-out and list that hub's outgoing transfers.' Also remove or soften the line implying that a busy payer is ordinary by default, and state that on this slice labeled transfers need not be ACH.
answer.system_fix: Add code facts about hubs. First, flag any account with zero inbound, out-degree of 10 or more and distinct recipients of 10 or more, and list its outgoing ids. Second, for each hub outflow, mark whether the recipient has any other activity (in or out) in the neighborhood. Third, mark the repeated identical-amount recurring pairs as 'recurring, likely scheduled' so the model can set them aside. Have a second pass report only hub-outflow ids to recipients that show onward activity, which gives about 7 of the 9 labeled ids (about 8 of 9 if tiny leaf recipients are added) while excluding most leaf-only rows. Output the hub-centred fan-out as the unit of analysis rather than individual transfers.
answer.risk_of_fix: Payroll, merchant-payout or treasury accounts with many one-way payments would be flagged as fan-out rings in ordinary neighborhoods. Listing all 20 hub transfers gives about 45% precision here (9 of 20). Filtering to recipients with onward activity is a heuristic that happens to fit this single case and could drop true leaf rows such as T1458 and T1484 or admit false ones.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Account 100428930 sent 20 transfers to 18 distinct recipients, so a fan-out candidate is visible. But only nine of its 20 transfers are labeled: T0233, T0600, T1003, T1025, T1262, T1458, T1480, T1484 and T1579. The rows do not supply a rule that separates them from its ordinary payments. For example, labeled T1458 and T1484 go to recipients with no other visible activity, as do unlabeled T0215 and T0265. The two visible onward paths, starting at T1262 and T1579, have substantially mismatched amounts and cannot establish which legs belong to the ring. None of the nine labeled transfers is ACH.

That missed the labeled fan-out, but their reluctance to flag all 20 hub payments was justified: these rows alone cannot recover the exact nine labeled IDs.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Assess a sender with many distinct recipients as a fan-out candidate even without loops, bursts, inbound funding or matched onward amounts; do not label every outgoing transfer illicit solely because it shares that sender. If the rows cannot distinguish the scheme's legs from ordinary payments, state that the exact IDs are not recoverable and request more context." Remove or explicitly limit the main-slice ACH-label fact when evaluating a held-out slice.
answer.system_fix: Add a candidate-review pass for unusually high distinct-recipient counts, here 18 for 100428930. Route candidates lacking transfer-level discriminators to an insufficient-evidence outcome or broader-context review, not an automatic laundering alert.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ordinary high-volume payers would receive more review. Treating candidate status as an alert, or flagging all 20 payments, would create false positives.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The hub is visible: account 100428930 sent 20 transfers to 18 distinct accounts and received none, which is a fan-out shape. The nine labeled transfers are all outflows from that hub: T0233, T0600, T1003, T1025, T1262, T1458, T1480, T1484, T1579. Two labeled outflows have downstream pass-throughs in the computed facts: T1262 (100428930->80D61AF60) followed by T1363 (80D61AF60->80D815530), and T1579 (100428930->80D5E56F0) followed by T1727/T1809/T1810 to 80D82E2E0. However, the exact nine are not separable from the other eleven 100428930 outflows using only these row features; no inbound, cycle, or burst marks them.

They also discounted the downstream pass-throughs because amounts were mismatched, so they never treated the out-only hub as a fan-out scheme. This caused all six runs to flag zero of the nine labeled transfers.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'An out-only account sending to 15 or more distinct accounts is a fan-out candidate unless the data shows a clear non-laundering reason; do not dismiss it as a business payer merely because it has no inbound, uses mixed formats, or has no cycle.'
answer.system_fix: Add a second-pass rule: if no scheme is found and any account has in-degree 0 and out-degree >= 15 distinct recipients, collect all transfers from that account and ask the model to label the fan-out members explicitly.
answer.risk_of_fix: It would newly flag legitimate accounts-payable or marketplace hubs that pay many distinct suppliers, especially if the model cannot verify the business relationship from the given rows.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: All 9 labeled ids (T0233, T0600, T1003, T1025, T1262, T1458, T1480, T1484, T1579) are outbound from send-only hub 100428930 (20 sends to 18 accounts, 0 inbound). No other account's rows are labeled. Nothing separates those 9 from the hub's other 11 outflows (T0215, T0265, T0405, T0630, T0964, T1044, T1368, T1820, T1851, T2349, T2406): amounts overlap (labeled 10.85–41534.65 vs unlabeled 860.38–470576.50), formats mix Cash/Cheque/Credit Card on both sides, currency is Brazil Real on all 60 rows, from_bank is 070 throughout, and the 9 are spread 2022/09/01–09/07 with no 3-in-60-minute burst. The 4 pass-through facts cover only T1262 and T1579 and amounts do not match (1559.58 then 256045.73; 41534.65 then 519.23/1062.72). 0 loops. Exact membership of the 9 is not in the rows.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every run saw the fan-out and rejected it as a business payer: amounts from 10.85 to 470576.50, mixed formats and banks, ~10 days, no inbound funds. v5 then treated 0 loops and 0 bursts as failing every scheme test, so a slow fan-out could not be named. The prompt line that busy accounts are not suspicious licensed that dismissal, and the same features group all 20 hub outflows, so the models could not have listed exactly the 9 labeled ids.
answer.prompt_fix: Replace any rule that 0 loops and 0 bursts means no scheme with: Fan-out does not require a burst, a cycle, similar amounts, or one payment format; a send-only account paying many distinct recipients over several days is still a fan-out candidate — list its outbound ids and do not clear it only because it looks like a payer. Identical recurring payments on a stable pair are ordinary and are not part of that fan-out.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact send_only_fanout [{account, n_recipients, n_inbound, transfer_ids}] and stop the v5 confidence rule from auto-clearing when loops=0 and bursts=0. Do not add an ACH-only filter from the main slice: none of the 9 labeled ids are ACH. No local threshold splits the 9 from the 11 unlabeled hub outflows, so exact-id recovery needs a label outside this neighborhood; otherwise leave the system as none.
answer.risk_of_fix: Flagging the whole hub false-alarms the 11 unlabeled outflows T0215, T0265, T0405, T0630, T0964, T1044, T1368, T1820, T1851, T2349, T2406, and will flag ordinary send-only payroll or supplier accounts in other neighborhoods. answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled transfer is T0810 (801ABBFE0 -> 801ABC3E0, 1036.99, ACH, 2022/09/02 18:36). The bench note says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. Only 3 of the 30 rows are ACH: T0809 (801ABC430, 4019.18), T0810 and T0817 (801ABC340, 270.86). They hit 801ABC3E0 within 8 minutes. The other 27 rows are Cheque or Credit Card, so the format narrows the candidates to 3 rows. T0810 is also the odd one out against its own sender's history. 801ABBFE0 sends 19 transfers, all repeating fixed amounts to fixed payees and all by Cheque or Credit Card. T0810 is its only ACH, its only transfer to 801ABC3E0, and its only one-off amount. T0809 and T0817 come from senders with one row each, so they have no baseline to deviate from. There is no loop, no pass-through and no structure. The data does not prove T0810 is laundering. At best it is the one row that breaks a busy sender's habit, inside the only ACH cluster, which makes it a 1-in-3 to 1-in-2 pick.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most runs saw a 'busy accounts with recurring payments, no loops, no pass-through' neighborhood and said ordinary, which is correct for every structural pattern in the prompt. A 'lone' ring has no structure to find, so the structural facts could not help. Nobody used the format limit: the prompt lists it as a known limit, but no run turned it into 'the 3 ACH rows are the only candidates'. Sonnet v1 did spot the fan-in and the ACH burst but flagged all 12 inbound rows, so it got T0810 by luck and kept the other 11 as noise. It also dismissed the recurring payments as scheduled, which was right for them.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A lone ring is one transfer with no structure. If the neighborhood is mostly Cheque or Credit Card and contains a few ACH rows, treat the ACH rows as the only candidates. Of those, flag at most one transfer, the one that departs from its sender's habit (a new payee, a new format, an amount that does not repeat). Give it low confidence. Do not flag recurring fixed-amount payments or the other rows of a fan-in.'
answer.system_fix: Add per-transfer code facts: (a) a list of ACH rows when ACH is a minority format, (b) a 'novelty' flag per row for a sender-recipient pair, format and amount that appear only once in the neighborhood while the sender's other rows repeat, and (c) a 'recurring' flag for rows with an identical amount and pair seen 3 or more times. Add a second pass that picks at most one row from the novel-ACH set. That turns the lone case into a per-transfer ranking, not a neighborhood verdict.
answer.risk_of_fix: It leans on a synthetic-data artifact (laundering = ACH) and would not hold on real data, where ACH is ordinary. On this bench it will flag one row in any neighborhood with a stray ACH transfer from a busy sender. Most of those neighborhoods are ordinary, so false alarms rise. Here the 1-in-3 guess could just as easily land on T0809 or T0817, which would be a wrong accusation of a real customer in production terms.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The laundering ring is account 100428930's fan-out: all 9 labeled transfers (T0233, T0600, T1003, T1025, T1262, T1458, T1480, T1484, T1579) are sends from 100428930, which sent 20 transfers to 18 distinct accounts and received nothing. So the hub is identifiable: a zero-inbound account spraying money to 18 counterparties is the only candidate ring in the data. What is NOT recoverable is which of its 20 sends are the dirty 9: the labeled ones span Cash, Cheque and Credit Card, amounts from 10.85 (T1484) to 41534.65 (T1579), and 10 different banks, and they are indistinguishable from its 11 unlabeled sends (e.g. T0215 for 10078.57 Cheque, T0630 for 470576.5 Cheque, T2406 for 112419.2). Worse, the prompt's stated bench hint says labeled transfers are ACH; none of the 9 labeled transfers here are ACH, so the hint actively steered models away from the truth.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every model correctly located 100428930 as the only suspicious structure and then talked itself out of it by applying a 'busy business payer' benign explanation, exactly the failure mode the prompt invites with 'busy accounts are not by themselves suspicious.' The models also leaned on the computed facts (0 loops, 0 bursts) and the known-limits hint (labeled = ACH) to conclude 'scheme tests not met,' even though the fan-out pattern only requires one account sending to many, which was satisfied. The v5 run even said confidence medium on 'ordinary' while describing the true hub.
answer.prompt_fix: Remove or qualify the bench hint 'every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH' (it is false for heldout slices and suppresses detection), and add: 'A fan-out verdict does not require loops, bursts, or amount matching; a single account that sends to many distinct accounts while receiving nothing is sufficient grounds to flag it as a fan-out ring and list its outgoing transfers, even if it could be an ordinary payer - say so and flag it anyway.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact 'zero-inbound high-fan-out sources' (accounts with sent>=N to >=M distinct accounts and 0 received) as an explicit candidate-scheme line, so the hub is presented as a named suspect rather than one row in a busiest-accounts table; in evaluation, score ring detection at the account level so flagging all of 100428930's outgoing transfers counts as a hit rather than penalizing the 11 clean ids.
answer.risk_of_fix: Any genuine payroll or vendor-disbursement account (zero inbound in-window, many counterparties) would now be flagged as fan-out, raising false positives on exactly the 'ordinary busy payer' neighborhoods the prompt currently protects; flagging all 20 sends of the hub also means 11 clean transfers get accused even when the verdict is right.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The stated dataset prior narrows the labeled transfer to the three ACH rows, T0809, T0810 and T0817. T0810 is distinctive because it is the only ACH among 801ABBFE0's 19 outgoing transfers; that sender otherwise makes largely repeated payments to fixed recipients. But the rows contain no evidence that makes T0810 laundering rather than an ordinary change of payment format. The exact label cannot be established from these transfers.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated the absence of loops or pass-through, and the prevalence of recurring payments, as grounds to clear the entire neighborhood. Those observations describe the neighborhood but cannot rule out a single labeled transfer. The v1 fan-in verdict made the opposite error: it included 11 unlabeled payments with T0810.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "A lone labeled transfer can occur within otherwise ordinary activity; assess unusual individual rows separately, but do not flag a transfer solely because it is ACH or part of a brief fan-in."
answer.system_fix: Add a row-level payment-format-novelty fact: T0810 is 801ABBFE0's only ACH in 19 outgoing transfers. Route such rows for targeted review rather than automatically declaring a ring; exact identification requires independent transaction-level evidence.
answer.risk_of_fix: Ordinary customers can switch payment formats. Automatically flagging a sender's first ACH would create false accusations; review alone cannot recover the dataset label with certainty.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0810 is one of only three ACH transfers in the 30 rows, all inbound to 801ABC3E0 within 8 minutes: T0809 (ACH, 4019.18), T0810 (ACH, 1036.99), T0817 (ACH, 270.86). The known bench rule says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH, so the true label must be among those three ACH rows, but the local data alone cannot separate T0810 from T0809 or T0817: there is no loop, pass-through, or amount anomaly that singles it out.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v2 and later models treated the repeated identical amounts as ordinary scheduled payments and then used the absence of loops and pass-through as a near-certain exoneration, so they ignored the payment-format signal. Claude v1 did notice the fan-in and flagged all 12 incoming transfers to 801ABC3E0, but because 11 of them were unlabeled recurring Cheque/Credit Card payments, that run was too broad and low confidence.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A lone ring is a single transfer; absence of loops, pass-through, fan-in/fan-out, or chains does not rule out laundering. In this synthetic slice, a lone ACH transfer is a strong laundering signal, so if a neighborhood is mostly Cheque/Credit Card recurring traffic and contains very few ACH transfers, list each ACH transfer id as a candidate ring rather than dismissing the neighborhood as ordinary.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact listing ACH ids and their burst: 'ACH-only burst into 801ABC3E0: T0809, T0810, T0817 within 8 minutes; in this bench labeled laundering transfers are ACH.' Then add a second pass that, when loops and pass-through are absent, scores ACH rows individually instead of requiring a structural pattern.
answer.risk_of_fix: It would over-flag ordinary ACH payments, especially T0809 and T0817 in this same burst, and outside this synthetic slice it would create many false alarms on legitimate ACH payroll, vendor, or invoice batches.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The single labeled transfer T0810 has no unique structural signature — the neighborhood genuinely reads 'lone': 0 loops, 0 pass-through, heavy recurring identical-amount traffic. The only discriminating evidence is the bench's own stated priors: every labeled laundering transfer in this slice is ACH, and T0810 is one of only 3 ACH rows (T0809, T0810, T0817), all arriving at the collector account 801ABC3E0 (bank 014325) within an 8-minute burst on 2022/09/02 from 3 distinct payer banks. So T0810 is recoverable only as a member of a 3-candidate set defined by the ACH tell plus the burst fact, not as an individually identifiable row.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v2+ models leaned on the computed facts (0 loops, 0 pass-through, dominant recurring fixed-amount payments) and reasonably concluded 'ordinary', because a lone labeled transfer produces no graph structure for them to find. They also failed to exploit the prompt's own known-limit hint that labeled rows are ACH: only 3 of 30 rows are ACH and they form the single computed inbound burst, which should have concentrated suspicion on T0809/T0810/T0817. Ironically v1 (raw rows) flagged 12 ids including T0810 via the fan-in reading, and the added facts in v2 argued the model out of its one lucky hit.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'When the facts show no scheme structure but a small minority of rows share the laundering-typical payment format (here: ACH) and coincide with a computed burst into a collector account, report a low-confidence lone suspect: name those specific transfer ids as candidates rather than answering ordinary with zero ids.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact to the fact block: 'format-tell candidates': rows whose payment_format equals the slice's labeled-laundering format AND that participate in any computed burst or fan-in, listed with ids (here it would output T0809, T0810, T0817). This is a cheap set-intersection over facts already computed.
answer.risk_of_fix: On ordinary neighborhoods that happen to contain a small ACH burst (e.g. a payroll batch), the model would now emit low-confidence candidate ids instead of a clean 'ordinary', raising false-positive ids and possibly flipping some verdicts to ring; mitigated by requiring both the format tell and a burst/fan-in, and by keeping confidence low so downstream triage treats it as a watchlist hint, not an accusation.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Only T0810 is labeled, and it is the sole sender-baseline break: 801ABBFE0's other 18 payments repeat 3481.94 and 780.44 to 813338210, 246.65 to 80DAE8940, and 754.59/245.17 to 802B3D770 on Cheque or Credit Card, while T0810 (2022/09/02 18:36, 1036.99, ACH, bank 010 to 014325) is that sender's only ACH, only payment to 801ABC3E0, and only non-repeating amount. Nothing shows a cycle, chain, or pass-through (0 loops, 0 pass-through, no account both sends and receives), and nothing marks co-burst T0809 (4019.18 ACH from 801ABC430) or T0817 (270.86 ACH from 801ABC340) as clean, so the lone label is not entailed by the rows.

The prompt's warning that busy accounts are not suspicious pushed the tighter runs to ordinary.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: Lone needs no loop, chain, pass-through, or fan. If a sender otherwise repeats the same amounts on the same formats to the same payees, flag only the single transfer that is that sender's sole use of a new format, a new payee, and a non-repeating amount; leave that sender's recurring payments and any co-timed inflows from other accounts unflagged.

Consider lone only for ids on that list (in this neighborhood that list is T0810 only).
answer.risk_of_fix: A legitimate one-off payment from an account that otherwise pays recurring bills, especially a new payee on ACH, will be accused. The rule will not catch a lone transfer whose sender has no recurring baseline inside the window, and a looser outlier definition would start flagging unlabeled one-offs such as T0809, T0817, T0426, and T0434.

They explained the hub's busyness away as recurring payments, and the real signal is a single row-level outlier. No model scored individual transfers by size, format and uniqueness, so T1749 was never singled out. The 'lone' pattern was never considered, and the ACH hint in the prompt was not applied to the 2 ACH rows.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "If there is no structure, still check for a lone ring: a single transfer that is ACH, is far larger than the rest (several times the median), and does not repeat an amount seen elsewhere in the neighborhood. If exactly one transfer fits all three, name pattern 'lone' and list only that id; if several fit or none, say ordinary."
answer.system_fix: Add per-row code facts: for each transfer, amount rank, ratio to neighborhood median, whether the amount repeats, and whether the format is ACH. Then list 'ACH rows that are the largest and unique in amount' as a candidate-lone fact. Optionally run a second pass over those candidates only, so the model judges the single row instead of the graph.
answer.risk_of_fix: Many ordinary neighborhoods have an occasional large, non-repeating ACH payment (payroll, rent, invoices), so a lone rule would raise false alarms. Since lone rings are one transfer in a large pool, precision would be low. Keep it as a flag with a conservative threshold, such as at least 2x the next largest amount, and test the false-alarm rate on ordinary neighborhoods before shipping.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1749 is the only labeled transfer. Its €10,940.76 ACH payment is more than 2.6 times 800238830's next-largest outgoing payment (€4,123.05, T1895). This would surface T1749 for review, not automatically label it.

In this synthetic AMLworld data the labeled laundering transfers are ACH, so such an outlier should be reported as a possible lone scheme even when there are no cycles, bursts, or pass-through matches.'

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1749 (10940.76, ACH, 800238830 -> 8000FE520) stands out against its own neighborhood: it is by far the largest transfer (max 10940.76 vs median 505.18, next largest 4123.05), it is one of only 2 ACH rows in a neighborhood dominated by Cheque/Credit Card/Cash, and its counterparty 8000FE520 is a pure sink (received 5, sent 0) whose other inflows are tiny recurring amounts (27.10, 68.14). A one-off large ACH into a small-amount sink account is the only visible tell; there is no structural signature (0 loops, 0 bursts, no scatter-gather), so the label cannot be derived from shape alone — only from the amount/format anomaly plus the bench hint that labeled transfers in this slice are ACH.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs anchored on the hub account 800238830 and spent their analysis explaining its repeated identical outflows (4011.33, 224.61, 27.10, 68.14) as recurring payments — a correct reading of those rows, but it consumed all attention. No model compared T1749's amount to the account's own baseline or to the amounts flowing into 8000FE520, and none used the stated bench hint (labeled laundering in the main slice is ACH) to notice that T1749 is one of only two ACH rows and is the extreme amount outlier. The prompt's pattern list pushed models to look for multi-transfer structure, and a lone transfer has none, so 'no loops, no bursts' read as 'ordinary'.
answer.prompt_fix: Add one sentence to the question: 'Before checking for structure, check every transfer against its own neighborhood: flag as suspicious any single transfer whose amount is a large multiple of the neighborhood median or of its counterparty's other inflows, especially if it is also the only one using a different payment format — a lone scheme is exactly one such transfer, with no loops, bursts, or repeats.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact per neighborhood: for each transfer, amount / neighborhood median, amount / max of the recipient account's other inflows, and whether its payment format is in the minority (<10% of rows). Surface the top outlier explicitly, e.g. 'T1749: 21.6x median, 160x recipient 8000FE520's other inflows, format ACH used by 2 of 21 rows'.
answer.risk_of_fix: Any neighborhood containing a legitimate large one-off payment (rent, invoice settlement) will produce a high-ratio outlier, so the rule will create false lone flags on ordinary traffic if applied without the format-minority and recipient-baseline conditions; it may also push models to always accuse the biggest transfer even in truly ordinary slices.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair is the only two-hop path 80832A480 -T0959-> 805D535A0 -T1211-> 802D21780. The prompt never said a chain here is a two-transfer fragment that need not balance.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: A chain may be only two hops, a fragment of a longer stack that continues outside this neighborhood: if A pays B and B's only later outbound is to C, name that pair a chain and list exactly those transfer ids even when the amounts differ, the currencies differ, and the gap is up to 72 hours; a mismatch is not proof the path is ordinary.
answer.system_fix: Widen the pass-through window from 48 hours to 72 hours and add a sole-outbound chain fact that does not require an amount or currency match: middle account, inbound id, outbound id, hours apart, formats, currencies. For this neighborhood that fact is T0959 and T1211 via 805D535A0 (sent 1 / received 13), 48.3h, ACH/Rupee then ACH/Euro, which the current facts never showed.

Requiring both hops to be ACH and cross-bank, and the middle account to have no other outbound, drops the cheque and card recurring pairs but still false-alarms on a legitimate one-off ACH payment.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing in the rows singles out T1313. It is one ACH transfer of 1543.45 USD from 8135CAB50 (bank 0051222) to 8015DEDF0 at 2022/09/05 22:44. The models spent their attention on the 8022663B0 burst and on 80B97F460's recurring payments, and none discussed T1313. Adding a rule such as 'flag a single one-off ACH transfer into an account that otherwise receives recurring payments' would fire on most ordinary neighborhoods. If anything, tell the model to say 'ordinary' and also name its most suspicious single transfer as a low-confidence 'lone' candidate, kept separate from the verdict.

Optionally, add a code fact listing 'one-off senders' (accounts with exactly one transfer into a receiver that has repeated senders), and use it only to rank rows for human review, never to set the verdict. Treat lone rings as a separate low-precision review queue.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1313 is the only transfer from 8135CAB50: a $1,543.45 ACH payment to 8015DEDF0. Nothing in these rows distinguishes it as laundering. answer.evidence_in_the_data: Only T1749 is labeled (800238830 -> 8000FE520, 10940.76 Euro, ACH, 2022/09/07 21:03), 1 of 21 rows, shape lone.
