Identical repeats (4011.33 on T1098, T1340, T1562, T1990; 224.61 on T0925, T1100, T2393; 27.10 on T0704 and T2023; 68.14 on T0819 and T2282; 1554.53 on T0769 and T2139) are recurring payments. T1749 is the max and the only amount above 10x the median 505.18, and one of two ACH rows (T0316 is 29.22), but a large one-off ACH is also a normal payment. The label is not in the graph.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs said ordinary and flagged nothing because they required multi-transfer structure and correctly refused the hub, the unmatched pass-throughs, and the identical-amount repeats. The prompt names lone but gives no test for it, and it says most neighborhoods are ordinary and a wrong accusation is costly, so 0 loops and 0 bursts was treated as enough to clear the case. v5 even raised confidence to medium on that negative evidence; none of the runs cited T1749.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "If there is no cycle, burst, amount-matched pass-through, or repeated coordination, verdict is ordinary: do not invent a lone scheme from the largest amount, from ACH, or from a busy account, and do not flag any id to avoid a miss."
answer.system_fix: Take lone rings out of this neighborhood screener's recall denominator, or score them with a separate single-transfer model. Do not add an amount-outlier or ACH fact for the LLM to auto-accuse: in these rows that heuristic would point at T1749 only by a cutoff, and the laundering fact is still not in the neighborhood.
answer.risk_of_fix: Excluding lone from this task leaves a real single-transfer laundering payment unscreened unless another control exists. A prompt rule that flags amount outliers or ACH to 'catch' T1749 would newly accuse legitimate large one-offs (here T1895 at 4123.05 is the near miss; T0316 is ACH but ordinary) and will not catch lone labels that are not outliers.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing in the rows or computed facts distinguishes the labeled laundering transfer T1313 (2022/09/05 22:44, 8135CAB50 -> 8015DEDF0, 1543.45 ACH). It is a single ACH payment from a sender who appears exactly once, sitting inside 16 other inbound payments to the same sink 8015DEDF0. Its amount (1543.45) is unremarkable — larger than the 443.01/296.63 recurring pair but dwarfed by the clearly odd T0620/T0626 (~70k/73k). There is no onward movement, loop, or pass-through involving T1313, and it does not participate in either burst. If anything, the data actively points elsewhere: the 8022663B0 burst (~148k in 12 minutes) is the visually salient anomaly, and it is clean. The 'lone' label here comes from IBM's generation metadata, not from anything observable in this window.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs correctly described the structure — a pure sink with recurring-looking payments and one odd burst — and correctly refused to call it a scheme, because structurally it is not one. The ground truth is a 'lone' ring: exactly one labeled transfer (T1313) whose suspiciousness is invisible at neighborhood level. The models' reasoning was sound; the label is simply not recoverable from the evidence they were shown, and the prompt's own definition of 'lone' (one suspicious transfer on its own) gave them no tell with which to pick T1313 out of 17 rows.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the known-limits note: 'In lone cases the labeled transfer is typically a single ACH payment from a sender who appears only once in the window; if the neighborhood is otherwise ordinary, you may name one such transfer as a low-confidence lone candidate rather than flagging nothing.' This at least lets a model emit T1313-shaped guesses instead of a blanket 'ordinary'.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact the models never see: per-sender recurrence count and whether the sender appears anywhere else in the full file, e.g. 'senders with exactly 1 transfer in this window: 8135CAB50 (T1313), 8022663B0 (3 in 12 min)'. A second pass could then ask the model to rank one-time ACH senders with non-round amounts as lone candidates. Without cross-window information, T1313 vs. an ordinary one-off payment is a coin flip.
answer.risk_of_fix: Flagging the unique-sender ACH transfer as a lone candidate would raise the lone-recall rate but will produce false positives on every neighborhood containing an ordinary one-off payment (e.g. a single legitimate transfer from a new customer), and in this very neighborhood the same rule could equally have picked a 8022663B0 transfer, which is clean. Net effect: converts missed lone rings into occasional wrong-row accusations — acceptable only if lone candidates are reported as low-confidence review items, not accusations.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1313 is the only transfer involving account 8135CAB50 and bank 0051222; it is an ACH payment of 1543.45 to hub 8015DEDF0 with no recurring counterpart. All other inbound traffic to 8015DEDF0 is either the fixed 443.01 ACH / 296.63 Cheque pair from 80B97F460 or the three-in-12-minute burst from 8022663B0 (T0620, T0626, T0628). Since the bench says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH and a lone ring is a single labeled transfer, T1313 is the structural outlier; but the rows alone show no onward movement or launder-like topology, so the truth is only partly recoverable.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated the absence of loops, pass-through and fan-in/out as decisive, and read the repeated 443.01/296.63 payments as ordinary recurring traffic. They noticed 8135CAB50 only as one of three senders and never applied the 'lone' pattern to the sole non-recurring ACH from a new sender/bank pair, T1313.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A one-off ACH transfer from a previously unseen from_account/from_bank pair to a common beneficiary may itself be the entire 'lone' scheme; do not require loops, pass-through, fan-in or fan-out. If one transfer is the only row for its sending account or bank and is not part of that recipient's recurring amounts, flag that transfer id as a candidate lone ring.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact for each hub: 'singleton sending pairs: 8135CAB50/0051222 -> T1313 only' (or more generally 'one-off senders') so the model does not bury that account among the three senders.
answer.risk_of_fix: It would newly flag legitimate one-time ACH payments to a shared beneficiary, such as a single invoice or rent payment from a new customer/bank, so it must be treated as a candidate for review rather than an automatic SAR.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The data show a clean three-account chain 80382B300 -> 803B8BFC0 -> 80462D300, but nothing marks it as laundering. Mixed formats (ACH, Credit Card, Cheque) alternate on the same edge: T0822 and T1495 are ACH, T1307, T1492 and T1596 are Credit Card, and T1597 is Cheque. The bench notes say all labeled laundering in the main slice is ACH, so this fits ordinary traffic. The same amounts repeat on the same edge: 451059.34 in T1307, T1492 and T1596, and 1782403.66 in T0822 and T1495. T1251 and T1833 both carry 444807.01 on the same edge, as do T1597 and T1598 on adjacent edges. The repeats look like recurring payments or retries, not layering. Out-flows from 803B8BFC0 are about 2.2M against about 6.3M in, with no amount matching one-to-one, so the money does not demonstrably move on. There are no loops and no bursts (the 'facts' list 0). T0569 at 100.9M is the largest transfer, but it goes out of 803B8BFC0 to a leaf and is isolated. The truth is only partly recoverable: the data lack a positive tell for ordinary, but the absence of tracing, the mixed formats and the recurring identical amounts point to ordinary traffic.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most runs saw an A->B->C shape with 10 'pass-through pairs' and took it as a chain. The pass-through pairs are a cross product of every in-flow with every later out-flow within 48h, so they inflate on any busy middle account and do not test whether the funds were forwarded. They also ignored that the chain is cheque and credit-card heavy and the amounts do not trace. The v5 run got it right by checking amount conservation and the loop/burst facts, while v1, v2 and v4 let repeated amounts and a 0.1h gap (T1597 -> T1598) outweigh that.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A chain needs evidence that the same money moved on: an out-transfer close to an in-transfer in amount (within a few percent) and in time, and ACH format. A hub that receives repeatedly from one account and pays one other account, in mixed formats with recurring identical amounts and no amount match, is ordinary. Do not flag a chain from pass-through pairs alone.'
answer.system_fix: Replace the all-pairs 'pass-through pairs' fact with a matched-amount fact: report only pairs where out/in amount ratio is within about 0.9-1.0 and gap under a few hours, and add counts of ACH vs non-ACH rows on the candidate edges, plus a recurring-payment fact (same sender, receiver and amount repeated). Show 'no amount-matched pass-throughs' explicitly when there are none.
answer.risk_of_fix: Real layering that splits or fees amounts, or that moves through non-ACH formats, would be missed; the ACH rule depends on this synthetic data set's labels and may not hold elsewhere. A tight amount match would miss split-and-merge chains.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Ground truth marks only T1313 (8135CAB50 -> 8015DEDF0, 1543.45 USD ACH, 2022/09/05 22:44, banks 0051222/0123773). That row is a singleton sender with a unique amount, but it shares sink 8015DEDF0 with 16 other credits and has no loop, chain, pass-through, or co-timed multi-sender fan-in. It is quieter than the unlabeled 12-minute burst T0620 (70112.14 ACH), T0626 (73751.96 Cheque), and T0628 (4074.27 Credit Card) from 8022663B0. The other 13 rows are a stable recurring pair from 80B97F460 (443.01 ACH and 296.63 Cheque). ACH is not discriminative: 10 of 17 rows are ACH and only T1313 is labeled. Nothing in the rows or computed facts marks T1313 rather than the burst or the recurring set.
answer.why_the_models_failed: All six runs correctly read the neighborhood as a sink with no onward movement and treated 80B97F460's repeated 443.01/296.63 payments as scheduled traffic, so they returned ordinary and flagged 0 ids. The prompt's scheme list is structural; a lone ring has no such shape, and the only local anomaly they noticed (T0620, T0626, T0628) is not the labeled row. They therefore had no recoverable cue that T1313, rather than those burst rows or nothing, was the laundering transfer.
answer.prompt_fix: Remove 'lone (one suspicious transfer on its own)' from the patterns this prompt asks the model to name, and add: 'If the only candidate is a single transfer with no structural companions in these rows, return ordinary; do not flag a one-off sender or a unique amount (for example T1313) as a scheme.'
answer.system_fix: Stop scoring this neighborhood screener on lone rings. A lone HI-Small label is one tagged transfer and is not a property of the local graph; detect it only with features outside this window (the file's pattern id, or history/KYC not in these 17 rows). Do not add a unique-sender code fact as a lone trigger.
answer.risk_of_fix: Recall on true lone rings falls to zero for this bench, which is the right trade if the label is not in the rows. The dangerous alternative — flagging every singleton sender or the largest burst — would accuse ordinary one-off credits and, here, the unlabeled burst T0620, T0626, and T0628.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The bench's stated rule that labeled laundering transfers are ACH rules out the Credit Card and Cheque rows, including seven of the ten rows repeatedly flagged as a chain. The remaining ACH rows cannot be proved ordinary from these records. The apparent chain is weak evidence: the ten listed pass-through pairs are overlapping combinations of payments, not ten independently traced flows. T1597 precedes T1598 by seven minutes, but their amounts differ substantially; T0569 is a 100,942,875.25 Yen outflow from the supposed intermediary before any displayed inflow to it, showing that this neighborhood does not establish its funding history.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models treated repeated bilateral payments and temporal proximity as evidence that the same money passed from 80382B300 through 803B8BFC0 to 80462D300. They also described 803B8BFC0 as sending only to 80462D300, overlooking T0569 to a different recipient. The v5 model correctly declined to call a ring; the other runs let a plausible chain shape outweigh the lack of traced funds or independent suspicious evidence.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Do not call a chain merely because A repeatedly pays B and B later pays C; overlapping time-window pairs are not independent evidence. Absent a traceable, chronologically and quantitatively plausible flow or another independent suspicious indicator, classify that pattern as ordinary, and do not flag non-ACH rows when the bench guarantees all labeled laundering rows are ACH."
answer.system_fix: Replace the raw count of overlapping pass-through pairs with a chronological, non-overlapping flow check that reports amount compatibility and all of the intermediary's outflows, including T0569; enforce the stated non-ACH exclusion when selecting flagged IDs.
answer.risk_of_fix: A real chain that splits funds, mixes them with an existing balance, or falls partly outside the neighborhood could lack a close amount match and be missed. The flow check should therefore avoid treating a mismatch as proof of innocence.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The receipts into 803B8BFC0 from 80382B300 total ~6.29M (T0822 1,782,403.66; T1307/T1492/T1596 451,059.34 each; T1495 1,782,403.66; T1597 1,374,732.08) but its onward sends to 80462D300 total only ~2.27M (T1251/T1833 444,807.01; T1460 852,428.16; T1598 485,777.99), and no outgoing amount equals any incoming amount, so there is no amount conservation and no traceable pass-through. The repetitions (451,059.34 x3, 1,782,403.66 x2, 444,807.01 x2; T1084 and T1255 are an identical 2,471.57 cheque twice) recur on multi-day cycles, which is the signature of standing/recurring payments, not layering. Computed facts also show 0 loops and 0 bursts.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models pattern-matched 'one sender, one middle, one receiver plus close timing (T1597/T1598 seven minutes apart)' to the 'chain' definition in the prompt and ignored that the amounts neither match nor conserve — only v5 used the inflow/outflow gap to walk the verdict back. The computed pass-through-pair list actively fed the error by enumerating 10 candidate in/out pairings as if they were evidence, even though the '0.3 h / 0.1 h apart' pairs are just proximity, not fund flow. Several runs even hedged ('records do not establish the same funds were forwarded') but still returned verdict ring.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the scheme definitions: 'Before calling a chain, check amount conservation: if the middle account forwards substantially less than it receives and no outgoing amount matches an incoming one, do not call it a chain. Identical amounts repeating on multi-day intervals (standing orders, rent, payroll) are ordinary recurring payments, not layering; a pass-through pair listing is a candidate set, not evidence of fund flow.'
answer.system_fix: Extend the code facts with per-account inflow total, outflow total, and pass-through ratio (out/in) for the busiest accounts, and add a 'repeated identical amount across >=3 days' counter; drop pass-through pairs whose amounts differ by more than, say, 10% from the candidate list, or annotate each listed pair with the amount-match flag so the model sees the mismatch without computing it.
answer.risk_of_fix: A strict conservation rule will also suppress real chains where the launderer skims a fee at the middle account or splits amounts (smaller outgoing sums), and the repeated-amount heuristic could excuse smurfing that deliberately reuses round amounts; both are acceptable on this bench only if the rule requires repeated-and-non-conserving together rather than either alone.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled transfer is T2030 (80117E2E0 -> 80117E9C0, 2245.27, ACH, 2022/09/09 02:44), and it has no structure of its own. What marks it is weak. It is one of only four ACH rows (T1563, T1566, T2030, T2033). It sits in a small ACH cluster at 80117E880 and 80117E9C0: T1563 and T1566 on 09/07, then T2030 and T2033 eight minutes apart on 09/09. It is also the second hop of the pass-through 8005BC620 -> 80117E2E0 -> 80117E9C0 (T2004 then T2030, 2.4 h apart). T2033 is also ACH, but it is not labeled, so ACH alone does not separate the label from its neighbors. Nothing in the amounts, bursts or loop (T1566/T2033, 512.83 out vs 2706.72 back) singles out T2030. The label cannot be pinned down with confidence from these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Every large, bursty, repeated flow (80117E9C0 -> 8096E55E0, 80117E2E0 -> 80E0F9310, 80117E9C0 -> 801244C00) is a fixed bundle of identical amounts that recurs, so it looks like recurring payments. The one run that called a ring (sonnet v2) flagged those 12 large transfers and missed T2030 entirely, and the confidence rule then downgraded it to ordinary. A lone laundering ACH of 2245.27 has no counterparty fan, no loop and no amount match, so models searching for a multi-transfer scheme never looked at it.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A lone scheme is a single small ACH transfer with no structure around it. If the neighborhood has no multi-transfer scheme but contains ACH transfers (the only format the labeled transfers use here), name pattern lone and list the one ACH transfer that sits inside a pass-through or loop, rather than answering ordinary.' Also remove the instruction to flag repeated identical-amount bundles as layering, since in this slice they are recurring payments.
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact that lists the ACH transfers separately, with their counterparties and any pass-through or loop they belong to (here T1563, T1566, T2030, T2033, with T2030 following T2004). Run a second pass over only the ACH rows, asking which single transfer, if any, looks anomalous. Cap the flagged list at 1-2 ids so the large recurring bundles can't crowd out the lone transfer.
answer.risk_of_fix: Many ordinary neighborhoods contain ACH transfers, so a lone-ACH rule would produce many false alarms on real customers' routine payments. Here T2033 is equally ACH and unlabeled, so the rule could easily pick the wrong one of two or flag both. The ACH-only property comes from the synthetic labelling, not from real laundering behaviour.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The rows do not support a chain. T1597 sends 1,374,732.08 into 803B8BFC0 at 04:55 and T1598 sends 485,777.99 out at 05:02, but the amounts do not match, so this is not the same funds passing through. The other pass-through pairs also fail to trace one-to-one: T0822/T1495 are 1,782,403.66 in, while later outgoing amounts to 80462D300 are T1460 852,428.16, T1598 485,777.99, T1833 444,807.01 and T1251 444,807.01. The repeated sums look like recurring payments, not layering: T1307/T1492/T1596 are all 451,059.34 from 80382B300 to 803B8BFC0; T1251/T1833 are both 444,807.01 to 80462D300. Computed facts show 0 directed loops and 0 bursts.
answer.why_the_models_failed: They treated a three-account topology as a chain based on pass-through timing and repeated amounts, but ignored the amount traceability requirement. The 0.1-hour gap between T1597 and T1598 is not meaningful when 1,374,732.08 in becomes only 485,777.99 out. Fixed amounts recurring over several days are ordinary payment behavior, not evidence of laundering.
answer.prompt_fix: Do not call a chain unless the money can be traced: an outgoing amount from the middle account must closely match a prior incoming amount after fees or rounding. Recurring fixed-amount payments between the same counterparties over multiple days are ordinary, even if the accounts form a linear path.
answer.system_fix: Add computed facts for each pass-through pair: the amount-match ratio between the incoming and outgoing side, and a recurring-payment flag for the same from-account, to-account and amount appearing at least twice. Suppress the chain pattern when no pass-through pair has a close amount match.
answer.risk_of_fix: It could miss real laundering where amounts are split, merged, or commingled through a middle account so that inflows and outflows do not match one-to-one, and it may reduce detection of genuine chains that intentionally alter amounts.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T2030 is an ACH transfer from 80117E2E0 to 80117E9C0, linking the neighborhood’s two busiest senders. That makes it a reasonable lone-transfer candidate, but not an identifiable laundering transfer: T1563, T1566, and T2033 are also ACH, and the rows provide no source-of-funds or other evidence that distinguishes T2030 as illicit. The exact IBM label is not recoverable from these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models looked chiefly for multi-transfer schemes and recurring-payment patterns, so they missed the possibility that the only labeled transfer was a lone ACH bridge. Claude v2 instead flagged 12 large recurring transfers, none labeled; the later confidence rules removed those false flags but did not create evidence for T2030.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "After checking multi-transfer patterns, inspect individual ACH transfers for possible lone cases; use ACH format or a link between busy accounts to prioritize review, not as sufficient grounds to flag a transfer, and say when the exact label cannot be determined."
answer.system_fix: Add a second-pass review queue for individual ACH transfers linking active accounts, including T2030, without automatically labeling them. Exact-ID scoring for this case requires independent provenance or label information unavailable in the supplied neighborhood.
answer.risk_of_fix: Automatically flagging every ACH bridge would falsely accuse ordinary transfers; review-only prioritization avoids that but cannot guarantee recovery of T2030’s label.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Ordinary is recoverable from amount discontinuity, not from topology. 0 loops and 0 bursts. The alleged middle account 803B8BFC0 receives T0822, T1307, T1492, T1495, T1596, T1597 from 80382B300 (about 6.29M Yen) but sends only T1251, T1460, T1598, T1833 to 80462D300 (about 2.23M). No onward amount equals any inbound; the closest pair, 444807.01 (T1251/T1833) vs 451059.34 (T1307/T1492/T1596), still differs. Those repeats are the same figure on the same account pair, not a split. The 10 pass-through pairs are that one relationship crossed inside 48h (e.g. T1307 with T1460, T1597 with T1598), not ten tracings of the same funds. T0569 (100942875.25) leaves to a different account and forms no fan-out or cycle.
answer.why_the_models_failed: v1–v4 called a chain because 80382B300 pays only 803B8BFC0 and 803B8BFC0 later pays 80462D300, with T1597 and T1598 about 0.1h apart, and because the facts listed 10 pass-through pairs. They kept verdict ring after admitting the amounts do not match and there are no loops or bursts, reading duplicate amounts (451059.34 ×3, 1782403.66 ×2, 444807.01 ×2) as layering. A confidence hedge (v4) did not change the accusation; only v5's rule that most of the money does not move on returned ordinary.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: Do not call a chain or pass-through from A paying B and B later paying C, nor from a 48-hour pass-through listing. Require an onward transfer that equals a specific inbound amount, or onward transfers that together equal nearly the whole of that inbound; if no amount matches and the onward total is well under half the inbound total, return ordinary. Repeated identical amounts on the same account pair are recurring payments, not layering. Similar-but-unequal amounts (about 1%) are not a match.
answer.system_fix: Stop emitting combinatorial 48-hour pass-through pairs. Emit a pair only when the onward amount equals a specific inbound amount, or when onward amounts in the same 60 minutes sum to that inbound. Add forwarded_fraction for each alleged middle account (onward total to the next hop divided by inbound total from the alleged source); do not surface unmatched pairs.
answer.risk_of_fix: Raises false negatives on real stack fragments that skim a fee, convert, or forward only part of the inbound (chain_cut_short), which this bench's two-transfer chain definition can look like. A tolerance of 10% or more would not fix this case and could newly confirm it, because 444807.01 and 451059.34 differ by only about 1.4%.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing in the 27 rows marks T2030 (80117E2E0→80117E9C0, 2245.27, ACH, 2022/09/09 02:44) as the labeled row. It is 1 of 4 ACH transfers (T1563 3975.45, T1566 512.83, T2030 2245.27, T2033 2706.72); the other three are unlabeled. The only nearby inbound, T2004 (48.50, 2.4h earlier), does not match 2245.27, and no outbound from 80117E9C0 equals 2245.27. The only directed loop is T1566/T2033 (512.83 vs 2706.72, more than two days later), not T2030. Bursts T0766/T0767/T0770 and T2313/T2314/T2315, and repeated amounts 17589.75, 6670.92, 11120.38, 100222.13, 98023.08, are same-pair bundles, all unlabeled. The lone label is not in the neighborhood.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Five of six runs correctly refused the recurring same-pair bundles and the mismatched pass-throughs and returned ordinary, which is the right reading of the visible graph and therefore misses a lone label with no structure. Claude v2 called a fan-out on 80117E9C0's recurring sends and flagged 12 unlabeled ids, none of them T2030; v4's low-confidence rule then wiped that false ring. No fact in the prompt isolates T2030 from T1563, T1566, and T2033.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "If no amount-matched chain, cycle, fan-in, fan-out to several counterparties, scatter-gather, or mesh is present, answer ordinary and flag no ids; a single unmatched transfer, including a lone ACH, is not a scheme you can call from this neighborhood, and identical amounts repeated between the same two accounts are recurring payments, not fan-out."
answer.system_fix: Do not score lone-pattern slices as misses. Drop lone neighborhoods from this bench, or rejoin the slice to IBM's parent pattern before screening. Do not add an ACH filter or a bridge-transfer rule: T1563, T1566, and T2033 are ACH too, and 80117E880 already links the two busy accounts.
answer.risk_of_fix: Excluding lone cases means a true single-transfer placement known only to IBM's label will never be caught here. The prompt sentence correctly leaves T2030 unflagged on this data. An ACH-only or odd-single-transfer rule would false-alarm T1563, T1566, and T2033 in this neighborhood and ordinary ACH elsewhere.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T2030 (80117E2E0 -> 80117E9C0, 2022/09/09 02:44, 2245.27 USD, ACH) is the only labeled laundering transfer, and nothing in the rows or computed facts singles it out. It is a small ACH transfer buried among four other inbound ACH/small transfers to 80117E9C0 (T1566 512.83, T2033 2706.72, T1507 188.67, T1789/T2243 306.7). The only tells available are external hints, not structure: (1) the bench limit note says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH, and T2030 is ACH — but so are T1566, T2033 and T1563, so ACH alone picks 4 rows, not 1; (2) it sits in the pass-through pair T2004 -> T2030 (8005BC620 -> 80117E2E0 -> 80117E9C0, 2.4 h apart, 48.5 in then 2245.27 out), but that pair has heavily mismatched amounts and 10 other pass-through pairs look identical in kind. The surrounding 'loud' activity (repeated fixed-amount bundles T0766/67/70 and T2313-15, T0524/T0847/T1089, the loop T1566/T2033) is unlabeled. So the ground truth is a lone labeled row whose laundering role is not expressed in this neighborhood's structure.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models were asked to find a scheme with a visible shape, and this neighborhood's shape is genuinely ordinary-looking recurring traffic plus one invisible labeled row — the 'lone' ring has no fan-out, cycle, or chain to find. The v2 sonnet run did call 'ring' but flagged the 12 loudest transfers (the repeated bundles to 8096E55E0 and 80E0F9310), none of them labeled, i.e. it pattern-matched repetition-as-layering rather than the actual signal; v4/v5 then suppressed even that wrong answer via the confidence rule, which is the correct ordinary verdict but for the wrong reason. No model used the stated bench limit that main-slice laundering is ACH to at least narrow suspicion to the four ACH rows (T1563, T1566, T2030, T2033).
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'If you judge the neighborhood ordinary overall but the bench limits apply (e.g. main-slice laundering is ACH), still list up to 3 transfer ids that best fit the known limits as low-confidence candidates, in a separate field candidate_ids, without changing your verdict.' This turns the unused ACH hint into a recall mechanism without forcing a ring verdict on lone rows.
answer.system_fix: Add a second scoring pass outside the LLM: for any neighborhood whose structural reading is 'lone' or which the model calls ordinary, score rows by the known bench priors (ACH format in main slice, participation in a fast pass-through pair, timestamp near the labeled window) and emit the top-scoring row as a candidate. Here that pass would surface T2030 (ACH + 2.4h pass-through after T2004) ahead of T1566/T2033, which form a loop the priors do not reward.
answer.risk_of_fix: Both fixes raise false positives on ordinary ACH traffic: T1566, T2033 and T1563 would be flagged alongside T2030, and any neighborhood with routine ACH payroll or transfers would gain candidate flags, adding review load. If the ACH prior is slice-specific, it will also misfire on other slices where laundering uses other formats, so it must be gated to the main slice only.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The hub is 80B18E250. It receives 7 transfers from 6 distinct senders at 6 different banks and sends nothing out. Five of the six labeled transfers go into it (T0984, T1292, T1401, T1428, T1609), and all are ACH in US Dollar. Three of those senders move USD here although their other traffic is in another currency: 803A52250 is Yen (T0181, T0868, T0974), 802C6C120 is Euro (T0635, T0691, T0755), and 80AD1C820 is Australian Dollar (T0671, T0672, T0679). T0740 is the sixth labeled row. It is a feeder: 801997D20 -> 801998AE0 for 4109.34, which T1428 repeats exactly on the next hop to the hub. That link is visible only through the exact amount match. Two non-labeled rows look just like the ring: T0852 (Cheque, 3042.92) and T1429 (ACH, 7087.80, same minute as T1428). The data does not separate T1429 from the labeled rows. Nothing marks T0740 except the amount match.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The best runs (sonnet v2, gpt v2) found the fan-in at 80B18E250 and flagged 7 ids with 5 labeled, but both hedged, and they added the unlabeled T0852 and T1429 while missing T0740. The v4 confidence rule then turned sonnet's low-confidence ring call into 'ordinary'. v5 reasoned from loop and burst facts (no cycle, one-destination burst, small pass-through amounts) and ignored the hub's convergence. The ring is a quiet fan-in of mid-size amounts with no burst or loop, so the generic tells never fired, and the one real tell (a currency switch to USD) was never computed.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A low-confidence ring call is still a ring call: if one account receives from 4 or more distinct senders at different banks and sends nothing out, name fan-in and list the transfers into it. Only list ACH transfers, and add any transfer into a feeder account whose amount exactly matches a transfer into the hub.' Also remove 'no loop and no burst means ordinary' from the v5 reasoning.
answer.system_fix: Do not auto-downgrade low-confidence ring verdicts to ordinary. Send them to a second pass or a human queue instead. Add code facts: (1) hubs with in-degree of 4 or more from distinct banks and zero out-degree; (2) for each transfer, whether its currency differs from the sender's other transfers; (3) exact-amount matches across consecutive hops, such as T0740 and T1428. Choose the unit of analysis per hub, as ACH-only inbound transfers to that hub plus amount-matched feeders.
answer.risk_of_fix: More false alarms on ordinary collector accounts, such as merchants and payroll or settlement accounts, and on multi-currency customers. The ACH filter still admits T1429, which is unlabeled, and the amount-match rule can link coincidental equal amounts. The ring's six labeled rows cannot be reproduced exactly from the data, so some precision loss is unavoidable.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled transfer T2030 is the ACH payment that follows a small incoming payment from an otherwise inactive account: T2004 sends $48.50 by credit card from 8005BC620 to 80117E2E0, then 2.4h later T2030 sends $2245.27 by ACH from 80117E2E0 to 80117E9C0. The computed pass-through pair 8005BC620 -> 80117E2E0 -> 80117E9C0 is T2004->T2030, and 8005BC620 has exactly one transfer in the neighborhood. answer.why_the_models_failed: The models concentrated on the high-frequency, high-value repeated bundles around 80117E9C0 and 80117E2E0, reading them as ordinary recurring payments or, in v2, as a low-confidence fan-out, and missed the small one-off ACH link. They also treated mismatched amounts in the T2004->T2030 pass-through as exculpatory instead of using payment_format ACH as the tell.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'In this synthetic dataset every labeled laundering transfer is ACH; treat an ACH transfer as a candidate lone laundering link when its source account received a small incoming transfer from a counterparty with no other activity in the neighborhood within the previous 48 hours, even if the amounts differ.'
answer.system_fix: Add a derived fact to the facts block: ACH transfers preceded within 48h by an incoming payment from an account with exactly one neighborhood transfer; this yields T2030 via T2004. Require the model to explicitly accept or reject each such candidate.
answer.risk_of_fix: It could flag legitimate ACH payments following a first card payment from a new customer, especially in retail or correspondent contexts, and it will not catch laundering ACH with no such incoming one-off leg.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Five labeled transfers—T0984, T1292, T1401, T1428 and T1609—are ACH payments from distinct accounts and banks into 80B18E250. The sixth, T0740, is an upstream ACH payment of exactly $4,109.34, matching T1428 about four days later. The stated ACH-only property excludes the sink's cheque T0852. It does not distinguish the unlabeled ACH T1429 from the labeled sink payments by format, recipient or timestamp: T1429 and T1428 have the same sender, recipient and time. The amount match favors T1428, but the exact six labels and illicit purpose are not recoverable from these rows alone.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The fan-in runs found the right sink but treated all seven incoming transfers as ring members, adding T0852 and T1429 while missing upstream T0740. The stricter runs then turned uncertainty about the exact membership into an ordinary verdict, despite the convergent ACH payments and the T0740–T1428 amount match.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "For a suspected fan-in, assess each incoming transfer separately using any stated format constraint, and inspect upstream transfers for distinctive amount matches; do not include every payment to the sink automatically, and state explicitly when the rows cannot distinguish a labeled payment from a similar unlabeled one."
answer.system_fix: Add a candidate-level second pass that lists the sink's incoming transfer ids with format and sender bank, plus exact-amount upstream matches and their elapsed times. Keep the ring verdict separate from confidence in its exact transfer-id list.
answer.risk_of_fix: Exact amounts can recur innocently, while a genuine ring payment need not have a visible upstream match. Treating the match as proof—or excluding unmatched payments such as T1429 as a general rule—would create new errors.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The ring is genuinely visible: 80B18E250 receives 7 transfers from 6 distinct accounts at 6 distinct banks and never sends anything — a clean fan-in (T0852, T0984, T1292, T1401, T1428, T1429, T1609), and 6 of those 7 are the labeled set. The discriminator against the noise is payment format: all six labeled transfers are ACH (T0740, T0984, T1292, T1401, T1428, T1609) while the overwhelming traffic here is recurring identical-amount Cheque/Credit Card pairs (e.g. T1297/T1301 repeat T0186/T0181; T1413 repeats T0635), which are the synthetic dataset's benign background. T1428 also matches T0740's 4,109.34 exactly, tying the 801997D20/801998AE0 chain into the collector. What is NOT recoverable from rows alone: why T1429 and T0852 are excluded — T0852 (100428660 -> 80B18E250, Cheque) looks structurally identical to the labeled fan-in legs, and T1429 (7,087.80 ACH, same minute as T1428) looks like part of the scheme; only the ground-truth labels exclude them. So the ring's shape is recoverable, its exact membership only partly.
answer.why_the_models_failed: v2 actually solved this case — both sonnet and gpt found the fan-in to 80B18E250 and flagged 5 of 6 labeled ids (over-including only the structurally indistinguishable T0852 and T1429). The miss was manufactured downstream: the v4 confidence rule downgraded the correct low-confidence ring call to 'ordinary', and v5's tightened rule then reasoned itself out of it by demanding loops, multi-account bursts, and near-complete amount forwarding — criteria that fit chains/cycles but not a fan-in, where the collector legitimately never forwards anything. The bench's own hint ('every labeled laundering transfer is ACH') was never operationalized to separate the ACH fan-in legs from the recurring cheque background.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'Do not require a loop, a burst across 3+ accounts, or near-total amount forwarding to call a ring: in a fan-in the collector account typically sends nothing out, so absence of onward movement is expected, not exculpatory. In this dataset, recurring identical-amount Cheque/Credit Card pairs between the same two accounts are background traffic; a set of ACH transfers converging on one account that otherwise sits in a different currency cluster is a fan-in tell.'
answer.system_fix: Remove the rule that converts low-confidence ring verdicts into 'ordinary' (the v4/v5 downgrade); instead route low-confidence ring verdicts to a human-review queue rather than suppressing them. Optionally add one code fact: for each sink account (receives from >=3 distinct senders/banks, sends nothing), list its inbound transfers split by payment format, so the ACH-vs-cheque separation is explicit.
answer.risk_of_fix: Without the confidence downgrade, other low-confidence ring guesses (like gpt v1's lone T1620 cash call) will reach reviewers as alerts, raising false-positive workload; and the ACH-tell sentence could cause models to excuse genuine schemes that happen to use cheques in other slices, or to over-flag any ACH convergence such as legitimate payroll collectors.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled transfer is T0837 (8086FA900 -> 8086FA950, 2515.15, ACH, 2022/09/02 19:53). It is the only row from 8086FA900, and it sends back more than 8086FA950 had sent that account (T0677, 1489.6). The pair is also a two-way loop with T0677 and later T2216 (4026.88), and the two account ids differ by one character (8086FA900 vs 8086FA950). All of that makes T0837 a plausible candidate. It does not make it a certain one. Nothing in the rows separates T0837 from T0677 or T2216, which are ACH, similar in size, and unlabeled. The ACH format is also shared by T0662, T0677 and T2216, so format alone does not isolate it. The truth for a 'lone' ring is a single transfer picked by IBM's generator, and the rows give only weak structural support for it.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Most models were drawn to the 13 identical, repetitive payments from 801721CD0 and treated them as a schedule (v1, v4, v5 correctly dismissed this) or as a chain (gpt-6-sol v2 flagged all 19 rows). Claude v2 did identify the 8086FA950/8086FA900 loop and flagged T0837 (1 of 3 ids), but only at low confidence, and the v4 confidence rule then downgraded it to ordinary. In v5 the amounts not matching was used as an argument against laundering, even though a mismatch in a return flow is not exculpatory. Overall the models hedged, and the one correct hit was lost to the confidence rule or diluted by extra ids.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A lone ring is a single transfer. If one transfer closes a loop between two accounts (a return leg, e.g. T0837 against T0677) and you are unsure, still flag that single transfer id rather than answering ordinary, and do not flag the recurring-payment rows or the other legs of the loop. Mismatched amounts on a return leg do not clear it.'
answer.system_fix: Change the confidence rule so that a low-confidence ring with 1 to 2 flagged ids is not downgraded to ordinary but sent to a second pass or kept as a 'watch' verdict. Add a code fact listing the 'return legs' (transfers that close a reverse-direction pair, with the ACH flag) and the repeated-identical-amount payment series, so recurring schedules can be excluded from flagging.
answer.risk_of_fix: More single-transfer alerts on ordinary neighborhoods that contain a normal two-way exchange between accounts (refunds, reversals, paired accounts), raising false alarms. Since the loop here has three legs and only one is labeled, flagging 'the return leg' would also pick the wrong row in other cases (e.g. T0677 or T2216 rather than T0837).

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The ring is a fan-in to account 80B18E250. Five labeled transfers go directly into it: T0984 (803A52250, $1,161.00, ACH), T1292 (80DFCA010, $1,316.39, ACH), T1401 (802C6C120, $3,405.82, ACH), T1428 (801998AE0, $4,109.34, ACH), T1609 (80AD1C820, $10,003.75, ACH). Claude v4 saw the ring at low confidence and a confidence rule downgraded it to ordinary. Claude v5 applied too-strict structural tests (directed loop, burst to 3+ distinct accounts, pass-through of nearly the whole amount) that a pure fan-in does not satisfy, and the repeated identical-amount Yen pairs between 803A52250 and 803E65EE0 read as ordinary recurring business. answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A fan-in pattern - multiple distinct accounts at multiple different banks sending to one account that never sends money out - is suspicious by itself; it does not need a loop, a burst to three or more different accounts, or a pass-through of the entire amount. Do not downgrade a named pattern to ordinary merely because confidence is low.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed fact: 'sink accounts (receive but never send) with the count of distinct senders, sender banks, and ACH vs non-ACH transfers', and remove or soften the v4 confidence-downgrade rule so a low-confidence ring call escalates for human review instead of becoming ordinary.
answer.risk_of_fix: Legitimate collection accounts (rent collectors, marketplace payout accounts, payroll funding accounts) will now look like fan-ins and may be flagged. The recurring identical-amount Yen pairs could be over-read if a model applies the fan-in rule too broadly to any one-way account.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0837 is the only transfer from 8086FA900 back to 8086FA950, and it is ACH, as are all labeled transfers in the stated main slice. But T0677 and T2216 are also ACH transfers between those accounts in the opposite direction; the rows do not establish why only T0837 has IBM's laundering label. The ring verdicts instead treated the two-account loop or broader forwarding traffic as the scheme, flagging three or all 19 rows rather than the single labeled transfer. The v4 confidence rule then turned a low-confidence candidate into an ordinary verdict.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Assess whether an individual transfer could be a lone scheme even when its surrounding traffic looks ordinary; do not include other transfers solely because they form a loop with it, and do not treat ACH or a reverse payment alone as proof."
answer.system_fix: Add a transaction-level second pass that surfaces T0837 as the sole reverse-direction ACH for review, without automatically labeling it. Exact recovery of IBM's label requires transaction-level ground truth or evidence outside these rows.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T0837 is the only ACH transfer into 8086FA950 from 8086FA900, and it returns money to the account that had just sent 1,489.60 to 8086FA900 earlier the same day in T0677. Claude v2 briefly called a cycle and flagged T0837, but v4/v5's confidence rule downgraded the low-confidence cycle to ordinary. answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'A single transfer can be the scheme. If an ACH transfer is the only incoming transfer from an account that normally does not send to the receiver, or it closes a same-day two-account return even with mismatched amounts, flag it as a lone laundering transfer and list its id; do not require a larger chain or matched amounts.'
answer.system_fix: In the v4/v5 confidence rule, do not downgrade a low-confidence cycle/ring call to ordinary when it contains a same-day ACH return leg such as T0837; keep the offending id in the alert. Add a computed fact for 'unique inbound ACH to an otherwise single-source receiver' to highlight T0837.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only labeled row is T0837 (8086FA900→8086FA950, 2515.15, ACH, 2022/09/02 19:53). It is one of four ACH rows (T0662 1590.37, T0677 1489.6, T0837 2515.15, T2216 4026.88); the other 15 rows are a repeating schedule of 1165.04 cheques (T0674, T0996, T1023, T1130, T1722, T1800, T2211, T2342) and 351.95 cards (T0387, T1133, T1335, T1803, T2341) from 801721CD0 into 8086FA950, plus cash T2195. The two ring calls used the wrong pattern and the wrong rows (sonnet v2: cycle, 3 ids, only T0837 labeled; gpt v2: chain, all 19). v4/v5 then downgraded that low-confidence cycle to ordinary, which stops false alarms but cannot recover a lone label with no separating feature.

answer.system_fix: none. Do not add an ACH-only or reverse-flow lone detector: T0662, T0677, and T2216 are equally unexplained, so any such rule false-alarms them. Score this neighborhood as not recoverable rather than a miss, and keep the confidence downgrade that blocks low-confidence cycle calls.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The only two ACH transfers in the 31 rows are T1575 (80806B1D0 -> 8092F21D0, 13,397.19 CAD) and T1624 (8092F21D0 -> 801F12A80, 8,833.02 EUR), and they are the two labeled ones. They form a clean two-hop chain 5.9 h apart, and the currency changes between hops. The prompt itself states that every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH. Everything else is Cheque, Credit Card or Cash, and it is dominated by repeated identical-amount payments on fixed routes (T0580/T1703/T2328 at 225.84; T0206/T0862/T0976/T2501 at 555.87). The amounts do not match across the hops (13,397.19 in, 8,833.02 out), so no structural fact separates this from the other 'pass-through' pairs. The ACH format is the only strong marker.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The v2-v4 models were swamped by 13 listed pass-through pairs, most of which are recurring-payment noise or have mismatched amounts, and they dismissed the whole set as ordinary billing. They treated amount mismatch as disqualifying, even though in a cross-currency chain the amounts are not expected to match. Only gpt-6-sol v1 found T1575/T1624, and it hedged with a medium-confidence verdict. Later versions did not use the ACH hint that the prompt provided.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'In this bench, labeled laundering transfers are ACH. If a neighborhood contains ACH transfers, check them first; two ACH transfers chained through one account (A->B then B->C within a day) should be flagged as a chain even if the amounts or currencies differ. Do not require equal amounts for a pass-through.'
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact listing ACH transfers and any pairs of ACH transfers that share an intermediate account within 48 hours, so that the chain is surfaced rather than buried among 13 undifferentiated pass-through pairs. Also add a fact that tags recurring identical-amount routes, so they can be excluded from the pass-through count.
answer.risk_of_fix: It would flag any ordinary ACH-to-ACH relay as a chain. In slices where ACH is common, or on real data where this format hint does not hold, it would raise false alarms. It also leans on a synthetic-data artifact, so it would not transfer to production.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1575 (80806B1D0→8092F21D0, 12:02) and T1624 (8092F21D0→801F12A80, 17:56) are the neighborhood's only ACH transfers. They form a time-ordered two-transfer chain through 8092F21D0, 5 hours 54 minutes apart. That distinctive combination identifies the labeled pair, especially given the bench's stated ACH prior, but the rows cannot prove that the same funds moved onward or that either transfer was laundering.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Claude treated mismatched amounts and the absence of a cycle or further onward transfer as reasons to dismiss the chain, while giving recurring payments elsewhere too much weight. GPT identified the pair from raw rows in v1 but reversed to ordinary after the added facts emphasized nonmatching pass-through amounts. Neither v2 assessment gave sufficient weight to the fact that the two ACH rows themselves form the short chain this bench labels.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: "Before answering ordinary, inspect every ACH transfer for a time-ordered two-transfer chain through a shared account; if the neighborhood's only ACH transfers form that chain, assess those two IDs together even when amounts or currencies differ, and do not require a cycle or third hop. ACH alone is not grounds to flag a transfer."
answer.system_fix: Add a code fact listing pairs of consecutive ACH transfers that share an intermediate account, with elapsed time and both IDs; keep it as a candidate-generation fact, not an automatic laundering verdict.
answer.risk_of_fix: Two unrelated, legitimate ACH payments through the same account could form the same short chain and be falsely flagged. The main-slice observation that labeled transfers are ACH does not mean every ACH transfer is labeled.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: Nothing in the rows separates the labeled transfer T0837 (2022/09/02 19:53, 8086FA900 -> 8086FA950, 2515.15, ACH) from its unlabeled counterparts. It is one edge of a 2-account back-and-forth with T0677 and T2216 (8086FA950 -> 8086FA900), and IBM labeled only T0837 in that loop, so any structural rule that fires on T0837 must also fire on at least one unlabeled transfer. The bench hints do not help either: the 'every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH' tell matches 4 rows here (T0662, T0677, T0837, T2216), and the late-date tell is useless because everything is before 2022-09-10. There is no burst, no fan-out, no matching-amount chain; the lone label is a dataset annotation, not a visible structure.
answer.why_the_models_failed: Models faced an impossible disjunction: call the whole thing ordinary (v1, v4, v5) and miss the ring, or call the loop/chain a ring (v2 runs) and flag unlabeled rows along with T0837 — openai/gpt-6-sol v2 flagged all 19 ids to catch 1, and claude v2 flagged 3 of which 2 were wrong. The dominating visual signal (13 identical 1165.04/351.95 payments from 801721CD0) pulled models toward 'recurring payments, ordinary', while the only weak counter-signal (the 8086FA900 <-> 8086FA950 loop with mismatched amounts) was either dismissed as a two-account back-and-forth (v5) or over-extended into flagging the whole neighborhood. The v4 confidence rule actively converted the one correct 'ring' call into 'ordinary', making the bench strictly worse on this case.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the prompt: 'A single labeled transfer (lone) often sits inside a small back-and-forth or pass-through whose other legs look identical; if you see one anomalous transfer embedded in otherwise regular traffic, flag that transfer alone rather than the whole neighborhood or nothing — a ring verdict with one flagged id beats ordinary.' This nudges models toward the 1-id answer T0837 instead of the all-or-nothing choices they made.
answer.system_fix: Add a per-transfer anomaly fact, not just neighborhood aggregates: e.g., flag transfers whose amount is an outlier relative to that account pair's history and that reverse the pair's usual direction. Here T0837 is the only transfer going 8086FA900 -> 8086FA950 (direction reversal) at an amount (2515.15) that matches neither leg's typical value; T0677/T2216 follow the pair's dominant direction. That asymmetry is the only feature that singles out T0837 from its loop partners, though it is thin.
answer.risk_of_fix: A direction-reversal/outlier heuristic will fire on ordinary refunds, corrections, and one-off return payments elsewhere in the bench, creating new false positives on ordinary neighborhoods with a single counter-flow transfer. The prompt change toward 'flag one suspicious id' also invites models to pin a lone id on every borderline neighborhood, raising false-alarm rates where most slices are ordinary.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T1575 and T1624 are the only two ACH transfers in the neighborhood, and they form a two-hop chain: T1575 80806B1D0 -> 8092F21D0 (CAD 13,397.19) and T1624 8092F21D0 -> 801F12A80 (EUR 8,833.02) about 5.9 hours later. The code facts list 8092F21D0 as a pass-through and include the pass-through pair T1575,T1624. Every other transfer is Cheque, Credit Card, or Cash, and the rest of the traffic is mostly repeated identical-amount payments, so the two ACH transfers stand out.

They also treated the many repeated Cheque/Credit Card payments as ordinary and ignored the payment-format signal: the only ACH transfers in the neighborhood are exactly the labeled laundering transfers.
answer.prompt_fix: Add: 'In this synthetic data, labeled laundering transfers are ACH; treat an ACH pass-through chain as suspicious even if it is only two hops and the amounts or currencies differ, and do not require a cycle or exact amount match.'
answer.system_fix: Add a computed risk hint in the facts: flag any ACH transfer and any pass-through pair containing ACH, e.g. 'ACH_chain_candidate: T1575,T1624', so the model must address it before concluding ordinary.
answer.risk_of_fix: It could newly flag legitimate ACH payments, especially any two-hop ACH pass-through that is not laundering; keeping the rule tied to ACH plus pass-through reduces this, but some false positives remain.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: The labeled pair is the only coherent two-hop chain: T1575 (80806B1D0 -> 8092F21D0, 13,397.19 CAD, ACH) followed 5.9h later by T1624 (8092F21D0 -> 801F12A80, 8,833.02 EUR, ACH), i.e. money in at the hub and out across currency. Two code facts single it out: (1) T1575/T1624 are the only 2 ACH rows among 31 (formats: Cheque 17, Credit Card 10, Cash 2, ACH 2) and the bench's own known limit says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH; (2) they are the only pass-through pair with a plausible layer-and-take-out shape (hub receives, then disburses cross-currency within hours). But the amounts do not match (13,397 vs 8,833) and the chain is a cut fragment of a longer IBM stack, so without the 'ACH = labeled' bench hint the truth is only weakly recoverable; gpt-6-sol v1 found exactly this pair only by reasoning over format and timing.
answer.why_the_models_failed: The models applied an amount-conservation test: because 13,397 in did not equal 8,833 out (and the giant 10.5M cheques dwarfed everything), they concluded 'nothing is being relayed' and read the whole neighborhood as recurring billing. The computed 'pass-through pairs' fact actually amplified this by listing 13 pairs, 12 of which are amount-mismatched noise, training the model that pass-through == mismatch == benign. The prompt's chain definition ('money passed along A to B to C') gave no license for amount decay, currency change, or taking a cut, so the one pair that survived (gpt v1) was abandoned once v2's facts framed mismatch as exculpatory.
answer.prompt_fix: Add to the chain definition: 'In a chain, amounts need not match: layering typically shaves, splits, or converts currency between hops, and a cross-currency ACH hop shortly after funds arrive is itself suspicious even if the amount is smaller. Do not reject a chain solely because in/out amounts differ; reject it only if no temporal A->B->C sequence exists.'
answer.system_fix: In the code facts, annotate pass-through pairs with two extra fields per pair: payment_format of both legs and a currency_change flag, and emit a separate short list 'ACH transfers in this neighborhood' (here it would contain exactly T1575, T1624). Optionally rank pass-through pairs by (ACH + currency change + hours apart) instead of listing all 13 unranked, so the noise pairs stop diluting the signal.
answer.risk_of_fix: Relaxing amount-matching will make ordinary salary/rent pass-throughs (receive paycheck, pay smaller bills cross-currency) look chain-like, raising false positives on hub accounts; the ACH callout also over-fits to this bench's synthetic artifact (all-labeled-are-ACH) and would not generalize to data where laundering uses other formats.

answer.evidence_in_the_data: T2230 (8083BDEE0 -> 804895E90, 47289.97 Yuan, ACH, 2022/09/09 01:54) is the only ACH row among 31 and the only transfer that crosses currency: 8083BDEE0 otherwise only sends and receives UK Pound, and its only Yuan row is this one. It is by far the largest amount in the set (max 47289.97, next largest 26956.84 is Pound cheque T0099), and it is the only row where the 804895E90 hub receives a large sum (its other inbound is T1082, 232.64). The prompt itself says every labeled laundering transfer in the main slice is ACH, so the single ACH row is a strong pointer. Nothing structural marks it: no loop, no burst, and the 'pass-through' facts (T1959 -> T2230, T2191 -> T2230) are artifacts of busy accounts. The onward 804895E90 payments after T2230 (T2300, T2303) are the same 1004.23/1152.64 recurring amounts seen before it, so no layering follows.
